units.la: DISPVTATIO PRIMA. In qua DE LIBRIS S. SCRIPTURÆ CANONICIS.

units.tr: Status Controversiæ.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: SACRAM SCRIPTURAM, de cujus divina authoritate suprà egimus, Veteris & Novi Testamenti volumine,tanquam duobus illis uberibus, ex quibus germani Ecclesiæ liberi τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα sugunt,contineri,extra controversiam est.
units.tr: That Holy Scripture, whose divine authority we have discussed above, contained in the volume of the Old and New Testament, as in those two breasts from which the true children of the Church suck the pure rational milk, is beyond dispute.

units.la: 2. Hoc verò quæritur, an omnes illi libri,quotquot in Codice Biblico communiter reperiuntur, proprie sint Canonici, inprimis autem sequentes: Liber Tobiæ: Judith: Sapientiæ: Ecclesiastici: Esræ tertius & quartus: Maccabæorum duo: Baruchi: & Epistola Jeremiæ: Oratio Manassis: Adjectiones item ad Danielem & Estheram?
units.tr: 2. The question, however, is whether all those books which are commonly found in the biblical codex are properly canonical, and especially the following: the book of Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, the third and fourth books of Ezra, the two books of the Maccabees, Baruch, the Epistle of Jeremiah, the Prayer of Manasseh, and the additions also to Daniel and Esther?

units.la: 3. Pontificii illos, excepto tertio & quarto Esræ, quem ipse quoque Bellarm.rejicit, l.1.de Verbo Dei,cap.20. pro Canoni-cis agnoscunt.
units.tr: 3. The Papists acknowledge these as canonical, except the third and fourth of Ezra, which Bellarmine himself also rejects, in book 1, On the Word of God, chapter 20.

units.la: 4. Nos verò solos illos, omnes tamen Veteris Testamenti libros, quos prisca Judæorum Ecclesia, cui τὰ λόγια τ̄ Θεῦ [?] concredita sunt, amplexa est, quíque hebraicè scripti sunt,pro divinis agnoscimus.
units.tr: 4. We, however, acknowledge as divine only those books which are written in Hebrew, namely all the books of the Old Testament which the ancient Jewish Church, to which the oracles of God were entrusted, embraced.

units.la: 5. Novi verò Testamenti libros omnes in Canonicorum numerum recipimus; nihil morati illorum opinionem,qui epistolam Jacobi,Apocalypsin,aliosq; Novi Testamenti libros Canonicorum numero excludendos arbitrati sunt.
units.tr: 5. We receive all the books of the New Testament into the number of canonical books, paying no heed to the opinion of those who have judged that the Epistle of James, the Apocalypse, and other books of the New Testament should be excluded from the number of canonical books.

units.la: 6. Supra nominatos quod attinet, tametsi Veteris Testamenti volumini adjici soleant, eosque in Ecclesia, ad ejus,in bonis moribus,ædificationem,utiliter legi censeamus, divinam tamen & cum reliquis parem, ad stabiliendum fidei dogmata, autoritatem habere,minimè concedimus.
units.tr: 6. As for the books named above, although they are usually added to the volume of the Old Testament, and although we judge that they may usefully be read in the Church for the edification of good morals, we by no means grant that they possess a divine authority equal to the rest for establishing the doctrines of faith.

units.la: 7. Rectè enim ἀπόκρυφα[?], h.e. abscônditi dicuntur, quòd in lucem minimè proferendi sint, ubi de dogmate Christianæ religionis, incidit controversia.
units.tr: 7. For they are rightly called apocryphal, that is, hidden, because they are by no means to be brought out into the light when a controversy arises concerning a doctrine of the Christian religion.

units.la: Confirmatio nostræ sententiæ.
units.tr: Confirmation of our opinion.

units.la: I. Omnes libri Veteris Testamenti Canonici, scripti sunt à Prophetis Spiritu S. actis. 2. Pet. 1. 20.
units.tr: I. All the canonical books of the Old Testament were written by prophets moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1.20).

units.la: Atqui supra dictorum librorum nullus à Propheta scriptus est: sed omnes post Malachiam Prophetarum ultimū exarati sunt.
units.tr: But none of the books mentioned above was written by a prophet; all were composed after Malachi, the last of the prophets.

units.la: Ergo non sunt Canonici.
units.tr: Therefore they are not canonical.

units.la: II. Omnes Veteris Testamenti libri scripti sunt stylo prophetico, seu hebraicè.
units.tr: II. All the books of the Old Testament were written in the prophetic style, that is, in Hebrew.

units.la: At libri illi non hebraicè, sed græcè scripti sunt.
units.tr: But those books were not written in Hebrew but in Greek.

units.la: Ergo non sunt libri Veteris Testamenti Canonici.
units.tr: Therefore they are not canonical books of the Old Testament.

units.la: III. Si libri illi Canonici essent, haud dubiè citarentus à Christo & Apostolis in Novo Testamento. Ratio; quia reliqui omnes citātur, exceptis solis Nahumi & Sophoniæ libellis, qui tamen reliquos Canonicorū librorū characteres omnes habet.
units.tr: III. If those books were canonical, they would undoubtedly have been cited by Christ and the Apostles in the New Testament. The reason is that all the rest are cited, except only the books of Nahum and Zephaniah, which nevertheless bear all the marks of the canonical books.

units.la: At nullus istorum citatur. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: But none of these is cited. Therefore, etc.

units.la: IV. Quorum librorum autores 1. Falsa: 2. Ἀ'σύγκριτα[?] & inter se pugnantia: 3. Pugnantia cum Canonicis: 4. Pugnantia cum Fide: 5. Pugnantia cum Pietate & syncero Dei cultu: 6. Pugnantia cum piis moribus, tradunt, & ipsi veniam scriptionis petunt, illi Canonici non sunt.
units.tr: IV. Books whose authors (1) report falsehoods, (2) are inconsistent and mutually contradictory, (3) contradict the canonical books, (4) contradict the faith, (5) contradict piety and sincere worship of God, and (6) contradict good morals, and who themselves ask pardon for their writing, are not canonical.

units.la: Atqui tales sunt libri illi, de quibus controvertitur, ut nullus sit, quin si non omnes, saltem aliqui enumeratorum defectuum in ipsum competant.
units.tr: But such are those books about which the controversy is, so that there is none in which, if not all, at least some of the enumerated defects do not apply to it.

units.la: Traduntur enim his libris
units.tr: For these books are charged with:

units.la: 1. Falsa, velut mendacium Angelo tributum Tobiæ 5. 18. 19.
units.tr: 1. Falsehoods, such as the lie attributed to the angel to Tobit (Tobit 5.18, 19).

units.la: 2. Ἀ'σύναρτα[?], velut Narratio de Angelo in urbem Rages ablegato, ut invitaret Gahelem ad nuptias, cùm in ipsa urbe Rages, in qua Gahel habitavit, Tobias cum Sara Raguelis filia nuptias celebrarit. confer cap. 4. v. 21. cum cap. 6. v. 9. & 9. v. 3. Sic nunquam conciliabuntur, quæ Maccabæorum l. 1. cap. 6. v. 16. de Antiocho animi angore extincto narrantur, cum iis quæ de eodem l. 2. cap. 9. v. 5. & 9. memorantur. Nec consistunt, quæ l. 1. Macc. cap. 9. v. 3. de Juda anno 152. regni Seleucidarum occilo[?] narrantur,cum iis quæ de eodem anno Regni illius 188. literas ad Aristobulū dante l.2.cap.1.v.20.habentur. Multum quinetiā diversi historia cap.10.l.2. de administratione Lysiae habet,ab iis quæ l.1.v.17.memorantur. Nec congruunt quæ l.1.c.4.v.36.&l.2.c.10.v.3.de purgatione Templi scribuntur.
units.tr: 2. Inconsistencies, such as the narrative of the angel sent to the city of Rages to invite Gabael to the wedding, although in the very city of Rages, where Gabael lived, Tobias celebrated his marriage with Sara, daughter of Raguel (compare chapter 4 verse 21 with chapter 6 verse 9 and 9 verse 3). In the same way, what is narrated in 1 Maccabees chapter 6 verse 16 about the extinction of Antiochus's mental anguish cannot be reconciled with what is recorded of the same in 2 Maccabees chapter 9 verses 5 and 9. Nor do the accounts agree: what is told in 1 Maccabees chapter 9 verse 3 about Judas, in the year 152 of the Seleucid kingdom, when he was killed, with what is held in 2 Maccabees chapter 1 verse 20, where letters are given to Aristobulus in the same year, the year 188 of that kingdom. Moreover, the history in 2 Maccabees chapter 10 concerning the administration of Lysias differs much from what is related in 1 Maccabees chapter 1 verse 17. Nor do the things written in 1 Maccabees chapter 4 verse 36 and 2 Maccabees chapter 10 verse 3 about the purification of the Temple agree.

units.la: 3. Pugnantia cum Canonicis. Id genus sunt in Adjectionibus ad librum Estherae: Narratio de Mardocaei somnio, quod capite 11.v.2.dicitur contigisse anno secundo Assueri, cum illud in Canonico libro c.2.16. rejiciatur in annum ejus septimum. Fabula de præmio Mardocaeo dato, propter conjurationis indicium,contra libri Canonici cap.6.3. De Rege Estheram torvo vultu excipiente, ut ad ejus aspectu prope exanimata conciderit, cap.15.7. contra Canonici libri cap.5.v.2. De Patria item Hamanis,qui in Apocrypho libro cap.16.10.Macedo, in Canonico vero cap.3.1.Agagæus seu Amalekita fuisse dicitur. De consilio denique Hamanis, Regnum Persarum ad Macedones transferre volentis; nec enim tum temporis ea erat Macedonici Regni autoritas,ut tale quid in animum inducere potuerit Haman. Ejusdem farinæ sunt, quæ in Adjectionibus Danielis,de sex diebus,reperiuntur, quibus Daniel in leonum fovea detentus fuerit,cap.14.v.30. contra Danielis cap.6.v.20. Historia item de Habakuk,prandium ad Danielem deferente; cum notum sit, verum ac germanum Habakuk non illo tempore, sed ante Nebucadnezaris in Judaeam expeditionem vixisse. Similiter alius & nothus Daniel in Sufannæ dramate fingedus erit, cum nemo tam sit hospes in S.historia,qui γνώσιον[?] illum Danielem tum temporis puerum fuisse credat, certumque sit, αὐτονομίαν[?] & judicia capitalia Judaeis in Babylonia minimè fuisse concessa.
units.tr: 3. Contradictions with the canonical books. Of this kind are the following in the Additions to the book of Esther: the narrative of Mordecai's dream, which in chapter 11 verse 2 is said to have occurred in the second year of Artaxerxes, whereas in the canonical book (chapter 2 verse 16) it is placed in his seventh year. The fable of the reward given to Mordecai for disclosing the conspiracy is contrary to chapter 6 verse 3 of the canonical book. The claim that the king received Esther with a grim countenance, so that she nearly fainted at his sight (chapter 15 verse 7), is contrary to chapter 5 verse 2 of the canonical book. Likewise, concerning the country of Haman, who in the apocryphal book (chapter 16 verse 10) is said to be a Macedonian, whereas in the canonical book (chapter 3 verse 1) he is said to be an Agagite or Amalekite. Finally, the plan of Haman, who wished to transfer the kingdom of the Persians to the Macedonians; for at that time the authority of the Macedonian kingdom was not such that Haman could have conceived any such thing. Of the same stamp are the things found in the Additions to Daniel about the six days in which Daniel was kept in the lions' den (chapter 14 verse 30), contrary to Daniel chapter 6 verse 20. Likewise the story about Habakkuk bringing dinner to Daniel; since it is well known that the true and genuine Habakkuk lived not at that time but before Nebuchadnezzar's expedition into Judea. Similarly, another and spurious Daniel must be invented in the drama of Susanna, since no one is so unfamiliar with the Holy history as to believe that this Daniel, who is called a judge, was then a boy, and it is certain that self-government and capital judgments were by no means granted to the Jews in Babylonia.

units.la: 4. Pugnantia cum Fide; quæ enim de Dæmone rivale agente Tobię 3.v.8.& quę Ecclesiastici c.46.23. de Samuele post mortem prophetante leguntur, Ethnicam superstitionem sapiunt. Itē quæ de Elia corpore suo reversuro Ecclesiastici c.48.10. traduntur, ex loco Malachiæ cap.4.23.24. male intellecto prosecta sunt,sicut Christus Dominus ostendit Matth.11.14.
units.tr: 4. Contradictions with the faith. For what is read about the rival demon acting in Tobit 3 verse 8, and what is read in Ecclesiasticus chapter 46 verse 23 about Samuel prophesying after death, savours of heathen superstition. Likewise what is delivered in Ecclesiasticus chapter 48 verse 10 about Elijah returning in his body arose from a badly understood passage of Malachi chapter 4 verses 23 and 24, as Christ the Lord showed in Matthew 11.14.

units.la: 5. Pugnantia cum syncero Dei cultu. Huc facit, quòd Tobias cap.8.8.Diabolum non precibus, sed artificio magico abigere docetur: quòd cap.12.v.14.officium postulandi preces & Deo offerendi, quod Scriptura soli Christo vendicat, Angelo tribuitur: quòd θυμιάματα & suffitus oblatio à Tobia Nephthalita peracta leguntur, quę non alibi quàm Hierosolymis, nec ab aliis quàm à sacerdotibus fieri poterant: quòd lib.Macc.2.cap.1. & 2. de sacro, de arca sederis, deque altari, talia docentur, quæ velut nugas ipsi quoque Judæi respuunt: quòd deniq; eodem libro cap.12.v.42.43.Judas sacrificium pro mortuis obtulisse dicitur, quæ sanè ἐθελοθρησκεία in ipso probari nequit.
units.tr: 5. Contradictions with sincere worship of God. To this belongs the fact that Tobit, in chapter 8 verse 8, is taught to drive away the devil not by prayers but by magical art; that in chapter 12 verse 14 the office of asking prayers and offering them to God, which Scripture claims for Christ alone, is attributed to an angel; that the burning of incense and the offering of smoke by Tobit the Naphtalite are read of, which could be done nowhere but in Jerusalem, and by none but priests; that in the second book of Maccabees, chapters 1 and 2, concerning the sacred fire, the ark of the covenant, and the altar, such things are taught as the Jews themselves reject as trifles; and finally that in the same book, chapter 12 verses 42 and 43, Judas is said to have offered a sacrifice for the dead, which certainly cannot be proved to be a self-chosen worship.

units.la: 6. Pugnantia cum piis moribus; velut, quòd Judithæ cap.9. facinus illud Simeonis & Levi amplissimis laudibus celebratur, quod damnatur aperte Gen.49.5.6. quòd Judith ad mendacia se comparat, iisque à Deo benedici petit, quodque simulat se morem gesturam, nefariæ temulenti Principis libidini. Eodè referri debet laudatio αὐτοχειρίας 1.Macc.6.& 2.Macc.12.
units.tr: 6. Contradictions with good morals; for example, that in Judith chapter 9 that deed of Simeon and Levi is celebrated with the highest praise, which is plainly condemned at Genesis 49 verses 5 and 6; that Judith presents herself as a liar and asks God to bless her for it, and that she pretends she will gratify the wicked lust of a drunken prince. To the same category should be referred the praise of suicide in 1 Maccabees 6 and 2 Maccabees 12.

units.la: Tandem, nonnullos autorum fateri, se ex proprio cerebro scripsisse, veniamque scriptionis petere, ex Prologo in Ecclesiasticum & ex coronide 2.Maccab.cap.15.v.39.40.liquet.
units.tr: Finally, that some of the authors confess that they wrote from their own brain and ask pardon for their writing is clear from the Prologue to Ecclesiasticus and from the conclusion of 2 Maccabees chapter 15 verses 39 and 40.

units.la: Assertio nostræ sententiæ contra obje- c-tiones Pontificiorum.
units.tr: Assertion of our position against the objections of the Papists.

units.la: Exceptiones Papistarum adversus superiores rationes invictas, leviores sunt, quàm ut recensionem, nedum refutationem, mereantur. Rationes verò ipsorum pro libris Apocryphis, paucis expediendæ.
units.tr: The objections of the Papists against the above unanswerable arguments are too weak to deserve a review, let alone a refutation. Their arguments for the Apocryphal books may be dealt with in a few words.

units.la: 1. Objectio. In Concilio Carthaginensi tertio, Florentino & Tridentino, libri isti Canonici dicuntur. Ergo sunt Canonici.
units.tr: 1. Objection. In the Third Council of Carthage, the Florentine and the Tridentine, these books are called canonical. Therefore they are canonical.

units.la: R. I. Negatur Consequentia. 1. Propter fallaciam plurium interrogatorum; alia enim ratio est Concilii Carthaginensis, alia duorum posteriorum, quæ nimis recentia & in multis palam Antichristiana sunt. 2. Propter fallaciam Consequentis; nec enim Conciliis habetur fides, nisi quatenus ductum Scripturæ sequuntur. II. Assumtum est ambiguum. Canonicus enim liber aut ἁπλῶς ita dicitur, quòd perfecta sit fidei & morù regula; aut κατά τι, quòd sententias & historias tales complectatur, quæ in Ecclesia, utiliter ad ædificationem plebis in moribus, leguntur. Atque hoc sensu Canonici appellati sunt in Concilio Carthaginensi, sicut ipse Cardinalis Cajetanus in fine comm. Vet. Test. inquit, Ne turberis[?] novitie[?], si quando inveneris hos libros inter Canonicos supputari, vel in sacris Conciliis, vel in Doctoribus: non enim Canonici sunt, i.e. regulares, ad firmanda ea, quæ sunt fidei, sed quoad canonem morum, quia ad edificationem morum leguntur. Adhæc, ut maximè Concilium Carthaginense tertiu, eos pro Canonicis agnosceret[?], Concilium ei Laodicenum opponeremus, à quo libri isti inter Canonicos non sunt recepti.
units.tr: Answer. I. The inference is denied. (1) On account of the fallacy of several terms: the sense of the Council of Carthage is one thing, and that of the two later councils, which are too recent and in many respects plainly Antichristian, is another. (2) On account of the fallacy of the consequent: faith is not owed to councils except insofar as they follow the guidance of Scripture. II. The assumption is ambiguous. A book is called canonical in one sense absolutely, because it is the complete rule of faith and of morals; in another sense in part, because it contains such sayings and histories as are read in the Church for the profitable edification of the people in conduct. It is in this second sense that they were called canonical at the Council of Carthage, just as Cardinal Cajetan himself says at the end of his commentary on the Old Testament: "Do not be disturbed, novice, if you ever find these books counted among the canonical ones, either in the sacred councils or among the teachers. For they are not canonical, that is, regulative, for confirming those things which belong to faith, but with respect to the canon of morals, because they are read for the edification of conduct." Moreover, even if the Third Council of Carthage did acknowledge them as canonical, we would oppose to it the Council of Laodicea, by which these books were not received among the canonical ones.

units.la: II. Obj. Multi Patres hos libros Canonicos appellant. Ergo tales sunt.
units.tr: II. Objection. Many Fathers call these books canonical. Therefore they are such.

units.la: R. 1. Falsa Consequentia; quia Patribus non creditur, nisi quatenus secundum Scripturam loquuntur. 2. Assumtum ambiguum est; non enim proprie, sed æquivocè & populariter Canonicos appellant, non quòd pertineant ad κανόνα πρῶτον, sed ad ἀποστολικανόνα[?]. Alioquin Patres Patribus opponeremus; à nostris enim partibus stant vetustiores & puriores Patres. Hier. in Prologo Galeato, Apocrypha nescit Ecclesia. Ad Hebraeos igitur recurrendum. Cyprianus in symb. Leguntur, inquit, hi libri, non ad autoritatem fidei confirmandam. Aug. de doctrina Christiana, &c.
units.tr: Answer. (1) The inference is false, because the Fathers are not believed except insofar as they speak according to Scripture. (2) The assumption is ambiguous; for they call them canonical not properly but equivocally and in a popular sense, not because they belong to the first canon, but to the ecclesiastical canon. Otherwise we would be setting Fathers against Fathers; for the older and purer Fathers stand on our side. Jerome, in the Galeatus Prologue: "The Church does not know the Apocrypha. Therefore we must return to the Hebrews." Cyprian in his Creed: "These books are read," he says, "not to confirm the authority of faith." Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, etc.

units.la: III. Olim in Ecclesia legebantur, & ex illis multa citata sunt. Ergo sunt Canonici.
units.tr: III. Formerly these books were read in the Church, and many things have been cited from them. Therefore they are canonical.

units.la: R. Negatur Consequentia. Lectionem enim quod attinet, non lecti sunt ad fidei confirmationem, sed ad morum conformationem. Legebatur etiam liber Hermes Pastor, dictus, in Græciæ quibusdam Ecclesiis, nec tamen ideò Canonicus est, fatentibus ipsis Pontificiis, inprimis Bellar. Citationem verò istorum librorum quod attinet, tàm ex illa non sequitur, libros istos Canonicos esse, quàm de Ethnicorum libris id pronunciari nequit, quantumvis à Paulo citentur, Act. 17.28. Tit. 1.12.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is denied. As far as their reading goes, they were read not for confirming faith but for shaping conduct. The book called the Shepherd of Hermas was also read in some Greek churches, and yet it is not on that account canonical, as the Papists themselves admit, above all Bellarmine. As for the citation of these books, it does not follow from it that they are canonical any more than it can be pronounced about the books of the heathens, however often they are cited by Paul (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12).

units.la: IV. Multa in his libris sunt, quæ fidem & pietatem fovent. Ergo sunt Canonici.
units.tr: IV. Many things in these books foster faith and piety. Therefore they are canonical.

units.la: R. Negatur Consequetia; quia ex tertio & quarto Esræ talia quoq; hauriuntur, qui tamen, Bell. teste, Canonici nō sunt. Ut verò Canonicus sit liber, non solùm multa, sed omnia in illo tradita, ad fidem & pietatem facere debent: sed contrarium supra evicimus.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is denied, because many such things are also drawn from the third and fourth books of Ezra, which nevertheless, as Bellarmine testifies, are not canonical. For a book to be canonical, not merely many things but all things delivered in it ought to serve faith and piety; but we have proved the contrary above.

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA. In qua DE S. SCRIPTVRÆ EDI- TIONE AVTHENTICA.
units.tr: SECOND DISPUTATION. In which concerning the authentic edition of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Status Controversiæ.
units.tr: The State of the Controversy.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: QVÆRITVR inter nos & Pontificios, quænam Editio Scripturæ authentica sit?
units.tr: The question between us and the Papists is: which edition of Scripture is authentic?

units.la: 2. Pontificii queruntur, nimium à nobis tribui Hebraeæ[?] Veteris & Græcæ Novi Testamenti: è contrario Vulgatam Latinam pro authentica & canonizata habent & obtrudunt. Bell.l.1.de Verbo Dei,c.2.
units.tr: 2. The Papists complain that we attribute too much to the Hebrew of the Old Testament and the Greek of the New; on the contrary, they hold and press the Latin Vulgate as authentic and canonical. Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 1, chapter 2.

units.la: 3. Nos verò Scripturam non nisi in fontibus Hebræis & Græcis authenticam esse statuimus; Vulgatam verò Versionem tanquam humanam & mendosam pro authentica minimè cognoscimus.
units.tr: 3. We, however, hold that Scripture is authentic only in the Hebrew and Greek sources; the Vulgate version, as human and faulty, we do not in any way acknowledge as authentic.

units.la: Probatio nostræ sententiæ.
units.tr: Proof of our position.

units.la: 1. In ea Editione S. Scriptura authentica est, in quâ primitus à Prophetis & Apostolis, dictante Spiritu S., est exarata. At non in Latina, sed in Græca & Hebræa Editione hoc factum. Ergo non Latina, sed Hebræa & Græca editio authentica est.
units.tr: 1. That edition is authentic in which Holy Scripture was first written down by the Prophets and Apostles under the dictation of the Holy Spirit. But this was done not in the Latin but in the Greek and Hebrew edition. Therefore the Hebrew and Greek edition, not the Latin, is authentic.

units.la: 2. Editio humana non est authentica. Atqui Vulgata Latina, quam ab Hieronymo profectam esse contendunt, humana est. Ergo non est authentica.
units.tr: 2. A human edition is not authentic. But the Latin Vulgate, which they contend came from Jerome, is human. Therefore it is not authentic.

units.la: 3. Editio mendosa,& plurimos errores grammaticos & dogmaticos continens, authentica non est. At talis est Editio Vulgata. Ergo authentica non est.
units.tr: 3. An edition that is faulty and contains very many grammatical and doctrinal errors is not authentic. But the Vulgate edition is such. Therefore it is not authentic.

units.la: Assumtum plurimis exemplis probari posset, sed brevitatis causâ aliqua solum proferemus.
units.tr: This assumption could be proved by very many examples, but for the sake of brevity we shall offer only a few.

units.la: Exempla errorum Grammaticorum.
units.tr: Examples of grammatical errors.

units.la: Gen.7.15. Ingressæ sunt ad Noë in arcam, bina & bina, ex omni carne,&c. Gen.13.11. Divisi sunt alterutrum à fratre suo. Psal.67.21. Benedictus Dominus, die quotidie. Matth.20.28. Filius hominis non venit ministrari, &c. Matth.22.30. Neq; nubent, neq; nubentur.
units.tr: Gen. 7.15: "They went in to Noah into the ark, two and two, of all flesh," etc. Gen. 13.11: "They were separated one from another, from his brother." Ps. 67.21: "Blessed be the Lord, day by day." Matt. 20.28: "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto," etc. Matt. 22.30: "They neither marry, nor are given in marriage."

units.la: Eodem referendae corruptelae Vulgatae Editionis, quae tametsi levioris sint momenti, nec haerelibus ansam praebeant, ostendunt tamen illam cum fontibus non congruere. Velut
units.tr: To the same category belong the corruptions of the Vulgate edition which, although of lesser importance and not providing an occasion for heretics, nonetheless show that it does not agree with the sources. For example:

units.la: Gen.8.7. Dimisit corvum, qui egrediebatur, & non revertebatur. Vox negativa non est in textu Hebraico.
units.tr: Gen. 8.7: "He sent forth a raven, which went out and did not return." The negative word is not in the Hebrew text.

units.la: 3.Reg.16.7. Hoc est, Jehu, filium Hanani Prophetam. Haec verba non sunt in contextu Hebraico.
units.tr: 1 Kings 16.7: "That is, Jehu, the son of Hanani the Prophet." These words are not in the Hebrew context.

units.la: Matth.6.5. Qui amant: pro, Quia amant.
units.tr: Matt. 6.5: "Who love," for "Because they love."

units.la: Joh.5.46. Credetis forsan & mihi: pro, Crederetis utiq; & mihi.
units.tr: John 5.46: "Perhaps you will believe me also," for "You would certainly believe me also."

units.la: Rom.7.6. Nunc autem soluti sumus à lege mortis, in qua detinebamur: pro, Soluti sumus à lege, mortui ei, in qua detinebamur.
units.tr: Rom. 7.6: "But now we are loosed from the law of death, in which we were held," for "We are loosed from the law, dead to it, in which we were held."

units.la: 1.Tim.6.5. haec verba, ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τ[?]ῶν τοιούτων, non exprimuntur in Vulgata.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 6.5: the words ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων ["withdraw yourself from such"] are not expressed in the Vulgate.

units.la: 2.Petr.1.16. Indoctas fabulas, pro, arte compositas fabulas, σεσοφισμένοις[?].
units.tr: 2 Pet. 1.16: "Untaught fables," for "fables cleverly composed" [σεσοφισμένοις].

units.la: Apocal.14.3. Nemo poterit dicere canticum novum. Graece μαθεῖν discere, non λέγειν dicere.
units.tr: Rev. 14.3: "No one will be able to say a new song." In Greek it is μαθεῖν ["to learn"], not λέγειν ["to say"].

units.la: Exempla errorum Dogmaticorum.
units.tr: Examples of doctrinal errors.

units.la: Gen.3.15. Ipsa conteret caput serpentis. Hinc Bernhardus, alioquin sanctus vir, homil.3. Maria abstulit opprobrium matris Evae, & Patri pro Matre satisfecit, quod promittitur Genes.3. Atuerò Pronomen in Hebraico textu luculenter indicat, non vertendum ipsa, sed ipsum, nempe semen mulieris.
units.tr: Gen. 3.15: "She shall bruise the head of the serpent." Hence Bernard, otherwise a holy man, in homily 3: Mary removed the reproach of the mother Eve, and made satisfaction to the Father in place of the Mother, which is promised in Genesis 3. But the pronoun in the Hebrew text clearly indicates that it should not be rendered "she," but "he," namely the seed of the woman.

units.la: Gen.4.13. Major est iniquitas mea, quàm ut veniam merear. Hinc stabilire conantur meritum de congruo, cùm tamen in originali textu nulla meriti fiat mentio, qui ad verbum expressus ita habet, Major iniquitas mea, quàm ferre possim: h.e. Major est poena iniquitatis meae, (metonymicè) quàm ut sim ferendo.
units.tr: Gen. 4.13: "My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon." Hence they try to establish merit of congruity, although in the original text there is no mention of merit at all; it reads word for word: "My iniquity is greater than I can bear," that is, "The punishment of my iniquity is greater (by metonymy) than that I may bear it by enduring."

units.la: Gen.14.18. Melchizedech protulit panem & vinum, erat ENIM Sacerdos Altissimi. Hic ex voce ENIM, quae tamen in textu Hebraeo non est, colligunt, panem & vinum prolata fuisse ad sacrificium, in figuram missae. Haec verò verba sequentia potius respiciunt; ideò enim benedixit Abrahamo, quia fuit sacerdos Altisimi. Quòd igitur Abrahamum & servos ejus, pane & vino refecit, regiae erat liberalitatis: quòd verò benedixit Abrahamo, sacerdotalis erat dignitatis.
units.tr: Gen. 14.18: "Melchizedek brought out bread and wine, for he was the priest of the Most High." From the word "for," which however is not in the Hebrew text, they gather that bread and wine were brought out for sacrifice, as a figure of the Mass. But the following words rather refer to it: he blessed Abraham because he was priest of the Most High. Therefore, that he refreshed Abraham and his servants with bread and wine was an act of royal generosity; but that he blessed Abraham was a mark of priestly dignity.

units.la: Exodi 34.30.Videntes autem Aaron & filii Israel, cornutam Moysi faciem, pro radiantem. Unde Moses duobus cornibus pingitur, non sine Judaeorum offendiculo.
units.tr: Exod. 34.30: "And Aaron and the children of Israel, seeing the face of Moses, that it was horned," for "radiant." Hence Moses is painted with two horns, not without offence to the Jews.

units.la: Job.6.2.Utinam appenderentur peccata mea in statera. Hinc occasio captatur extenuandi peccata, quasi divina ultio delictis sit major. At in textu originali non de peccatis, sed de aerumnis & indignatione sua loquitur Jobus.
units.tr: Job 6.2: "Would that my sins were weighed in a balance." Hence an occasion is seized to diminish sins, as if divine vengeance were greater than the offences. But in the original text Job speaks not of sins but of his troubles and of God's indignation.

units.la: Psal.2.12. illustre testimonium de Christo,osculamini Filium, sic depravatur in Vulgata,apprehendite disciplinam.
units.tr: Ps. 2.12: an illustrious testimony concerning Christ, "Kiss the Son," is thus corrupted in the Vulgate: "Take hold of discipline."

units.la: Psal.18.5. Vulgata habet, in Sole posuit tabernaculum suum. Unde Bell.l.3.de Ecclesia militante, cap.16.conficere conatur, externum splendorem & visibilitatem esse Ecclesiae notam. Verum juxta textum originalem sic erat reddendum,Soli posuit (Deus) tabernaculum in eis, nempe coelis, de quibus in superioribus versibus.
units.tr: Ps. 18.5: The Vulgate has, "In the Sun he set his tabernacle." Hence Bellarmine, On the Militant Church, book 3, chapter 16, tries to establish that outward splendour and visibility are a mark of the Church. But according to the original text it ought to be rendered: "For the sun he (God) set a tabernacle in them," namely in the heavens, of which mention is made in the verses above.

units.la: Ecclesiastis 9.1.Nescit homo, utrum amore an odio dignus sit? Hinc error de incertitudine amoris divini & salutis aeternae. Quòd si verò textum Hebraeum ad verbum exprimere velimus, sic erit reddendus,etiam amorem, etiam odium non scit homo (ex) omnibus (quae) ad facies eorum, seu coram ipsis sunt. Summa est, ex rebus externis ac corporalibus judicium non fieri de amore aut odio divino.
units.tr: Eccles. 9.1: "Man knows not whether he is worthy of love or hatred?" Hence the error of uncertainty concerning divine love and eternal salvation. But if we wish to express the Hebrew text word for word, it must be rendered thus: "Man knows not even love, not even hatred, from all things that are before their faces," or in their presence. In sum, judgment about divine love or hatred is not made from external and bodily things.

units.la: Esaiae 28.16.Ecce ego mittam in fundamentis Sion, lapidem probatum, angularem, pretiosum, in fundamento fundatum. Haec Bell. praefat. de Rom. Pont. ad Petrum refert, qui sit fundamentum, fundatum, i.e. secundarium, respectu Christi, qui primarium sit fundamentum. Verum postrema verba fundationem fundationis, h.e. fundationem fundatissimam, Hebraeorum more significant, nec de alio fundamento totus locus ille intelligi poterit, quàm de Christo.
units.tr: Isa. 28.16: "Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a tried stone, a precious corner-stone, a sure foundation, founded upon a foundation." Bellarmine, in the preface to On the Roman Pontiff, refers this to Peter, who is the foundation "founded," that is, secondary with respect to Christ, who is the primary foundation. But the final words, in the Hebrew manner, signify a foundation of foundation, that is, a most firmly founded foundation, and the whole passage can be understood of no other foundation than Christ.

units.la: Danielis 4.24.Peccata tua Eleemosynâ redime. Hinc commentum meriti de condigno. At hebraicè ita habet locus: Peccata tua Eleemosynâ abrumpe.
units.tr: Dan. 4.24: "Redeem your sins with alms." Hence the fiction of merit of condignity. But in Hebrew the passage reads thus: "Break off your sins by alms."

units.la: Lucae 2.14.Gloria in altissimis Deo: & in terra pax, hominibus bona voluntatis. Hinc error de libera voluntate & arbitrio: graece ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀνδρείᾳ[?]; at vox ἀνδρεία[?] Dei potius beneplacitum significat.
units.tr: Luke 2.14: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will towards men." Hence the error about free will and choice; in Greek it is ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκίας ["among men of good pleasure"], but the word εὐδοκία rather signifies God's good pleasure.

units.la: Ioh.4.10. Si scires donum Dei, & quis est qui dicit, da mihi bibere, tu forsitan petiisses ab eo, & dedisset tibi aquam vivam. Hoc quoque loco, ad stabiliendum liberum arbitrium, abutuntur. At in graeco est vox ἄν[?], quae non forsitan, sed utique, reddenda.
units.tr: John 4.10: "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me to drink, you would perhaps have asked of him, and he would have given you living water." They abuse this passage too, to establish free will. But in the Greek there is the word ἄν, which must be rendered not "perhaps" but "certainly."

units.la: Eph.5.32. Hoc est magnum Sacramentum. Hinc conjugium Sacramentum esse contendunt. At in graeco textu est vox μυστήριον[?], quae multo latius patet, quam vox Sacramentum.
units.tr: Eph. 5.32: "This is a great sacrament." Hence they contend that marriage is a sacrament. But in the Greek text there is the word μυστήριον ["mystery"], which has a much wider range than the word sacrament.

units.la: Heb.11.21. Jacob adoravit fastigium virgae. Hinc colligunt, adorationem creaturis quoque praestari posse. Sed rectius vertitur, Adoravit super fastigium virgae suae, h.e. virgae innixus. Cum quo pulcre consonat, quod Gen.47.31. Tunc incurvavit se, honoris sc. Deo exhibendi causa, ad cervical lecti sui, baculi nimirum, quem senex in manu habuit, summitate nixus.
units.tr: Heb. 11.21: "Jacob adored the top of the rod." Hence they gather that adoration can also be offered to creatures. But it is more correctly rendered: "He adored upon the top of his rod," that is, leaning on his staff. With this agrees well what is said in Gen. 47.31: "Then he bowed himself," namely to show honour to God, "upon the bed's head," that is, of course, leaning on the top of the staff which the old man held in his hand.

units.la: Heb.11.16. Vulgata habet, talibus hostiis promeretur Deus: pro, delectatur Deus. Jam vero iterum Vulgata versio occasionem praebet, erroris, de humanis meritis.
units.tr: Heb. 11.16: The Vulgate has, "God is propitiated by such sacrifices," for "God is delighted." Now again the Vulgate version provides an occasion of error concerning human merits.

units.la: Assertio nostrae sententiae contra Pontificios.
units.tr: Assertion of our opinion against the Papists.

units.la: Argumenta Pontificiorum duplicia hic occurrunt, alia contra puritatem fontium, alia pro versione Vulgata.
units.tr: The Papists' arguments here occur in two kinds: some against the purity of the sources, others in favour of the Vulgate version.

units.la: 1. Contra fontium puritatem.
units.tr: 1. Against the purity of the sources.

units.la: Ex Hebraico contextu Bell.l.2.de Verbo Dei, cap.2. sequentes corruptelas eruit.
units.tr: From the Hebrew text, Bellarmine in book 2 of On the Word of God, chapter 2, draws out the following corruptions.

units.la: 1. Esaiae 9.v.6. Hebraeus textus habet, Et vocabit nomen ejus: jam vero contendit Calvinus lib.1.Inst.cap.13.9. legendum, vocabitur nomen ejus.
units.tr: 1. Isaiah 9:6. The Hebrew text has, "And he shall call his name" (et vocabit nomen ejus). Calvin, however, contends in Institutes book 1, chapter 13, section 9, that it should be read, "his name shall be called" (vocabitur nomen ejus).

units.la: 2. Eâdem ratione locum Jer.23.6. cùm in Hebraeo sit singulare vocabit, Calvinus legit, & hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum.
units.tr: 2. By the same reasoning, at Jeremiah 23:6, where the Hebrew has the singular "shall call," Calvin reads, "and this is the name by which they shall call him."

units.la: Ergo vel ipsius confessione, inquit Bellarminus, turbidus alicubi fluit fons ille, quem ipse idem, ubiq; purum videri volebat, neque ignoravit, his locis meliorem esse editionem Vulgatam, quàm Hebraicam.
units.tr: Therefore, by his own admission, says Bellarmine, that fountain flows muddily in places, though he himself wished it to appear pure everywhere; and he was not unaware that in these passages the Vulgate edition is better than the Hebrew.

units.la: R. Fallacia est à non causa ut causa. Nec enim Calvinus Vulgatam probare, nec Hebraicam improbare voluit, sed ad sensum potius evidentiorem, quàm ad verbum, utrumque locum interpretatus est. Nec insolens est apud Hebræos, verba tertiæ personæ utrovis numero imperfonaliter sumi, & modò activè, modò passivè.
units.tr: A. This is the fallacy of taking what is not the cause for the cause. For Calvin wished neither to approve the Vulgate nor to disapprove the Hebrew; rather he translated both passages according to the clearer sense rather than the word. Nor is it unusual among the Hebrews for verbs in the third person, in either number, to be used impersonally, and sometimes in the active and sometimes in the passive sense.

units.la: 3. Psal.22.17. Textus Hebraici habent, Caari, sicut Leo, non Caru foderunt, cùm tamen nemo Christianorum sit, qui non legat, foderunt manus meas.
units.tr: 3. Psalm 22:17. The Hebrew texts have "Caari," like a lion, not "Caru" they dug, although there is no Christian who does not read "they dug my hands."

units.la: R. Non omnes Hebræi Codices ita habent, sed quidam: nec absolutè, sed cum variæ lectionis annotatione: nec semper ita fuit lectio; ut probat Franciscus Junius, R. Jaahob filii Cham, verbis, in libro Massoreth[?], litera Aleph Resch sic scribentis: In parte librorum emendatiorum inveni, scribitur Caru & legitur Caari.
units.tr: A. Not all Hebrew codices read thus, but some do; and not absolutely, but with a note of variant reading; nor was the reading always so, as Franciscus Junius proves from the words of Rabbi Jaahob son of Cham, in the book Massoreth[?], writing with the letters Aleph and Resch: "In part of the more correct books I have found it written Caru and read Caari."

units.la: 4. Psal.19.5.Heb. in omnem terram exivit linea eorum: cùm tamen LXX. verterint, φθόγγος αὐτῶν[?], hancq; Versionem retineat potiùs Apostolus Rom.10.18. Patet igitur, fontem hoc loco non esse purum.
units.tr: 4. Psalm 19:5. Hebrew: "Their line has gone out into all the earth," whereas the Seventy translated φθόγγος αὐτῶν[?], and the Apostle Paul in Romans 10:18 retains rather that version. It is plain, therefore, that the source is not pure in this place.

units.la: R. Negatur Consequentia; cùm enim Paulus eodem spiritu, verba Davidis de creatione & cœlorum motu, ad cursum Euangelii accommodet, instituto suo liberè alias voces accommodat: quod genus παραφωδίαι[?] non paucæ in N.T. extant, ut docent Parallelorum Franc.Junii libri.
units.tr: A. The consequence is denied. For since Paul, by the same Spirit, applies David's words about the creation and the motion of the heavens to the course of the Gospel, he freely adapts other words to his own purpose; a kind of paraphrase (παραφωδίαι[?]) of which not a few occur in the New Testament, as the Parallel books of Franciscus Junius teach.

units.la: 5. Desunt in Hebræo integræ sententiæ, cùm non desint in versione LXX. & Hieronymi. e. g. Exod.2.deest totù illud: Alium quoque genuit & vocavit nomen ejus Eliazar, dicens, Deus Patris mei auxiliatus est mihi, & liberavit me de manu Pharaonis.
units.tr: 5. Whole sentences are lacking in the Hebrew, though they are not lacking in the version of the Seventy and of Jerome. For example, at Exodus 2 the whole of this is missing: "He also begot another and called his name Eliezer, saying, The God of my father helped me and delivered me from the hand of Pharaoh."

units.la: R. Falsa est Papistarum assertio, nec probatur hoc exemplo; quia versus hic aliunde, nimirum ex Exod.18.4.cap.2. infarctus est, & ineptè quidem; Gerson enim primogenitus Moses multis annis præcesit Eliezerum, ut qui adhuc ἀπερίτμητος[?] incircumcisus erat, cùm Moses se ad reversionem in Ægyptum accingeret. Exodi 4.
units.tr: A. The Papists' assertion is false, nor is it proved by this example; for this verse is inserted from elsewhere, namely from Exodus 18:4, and indeed inappropriately; for Gershom, the firstborn of Moses, was born many years before Eliezer, who, being still uncircumcised, was at the time when Moses was preparing to return to Egypt. Exodus 4.

units.la: Novi verò Testamenti græcam editionem non ita incorruptam esse, ut semper Latina ad ipsum corrigenda sit, his exemplis planum facere conatur Bell.l.2.de Verbo Dei,cap.7.
units.tr: But that the Greek edition of the New Testament is not so incorrupt that the Latin must always be corrected by it, Bellarmine in book 2 of On the Word of God, chapter 7, tries to make plain by these examples.

units.la: 1. Rom.12.11. In græco est, [illegible, ~9 letters] tempori servientes. Rectius Vulgata, Domino servientes.
units.tr: 1. Romans 12:11. In the Greek it is [illegible, about 9 letters] serving the time. The Vulgate is more correct: "serving the Lord."

units.la: R. In probatissimis Græcis exemplaribus, legitur νυμφίῳ[?]: jam verò malè quod paucorum est exemplarium, ad omnia transfertur.
units.tr: A. In the most approved Greek copies it is read νυμφίῳ[?]; but to carry over to everything what belongs to a few copies is wrong.

units.la: 2. In 1.Cor.7.34. μεμέρισται[?] ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος[?], divisa est uxor & virgo: Latina rectius, Qui cum uxore est, sollicitus est pro rebus hujus mundi & divisus est.
units.tr: 2. In 1 Corinthians 7:34, μεμέρισται[?] ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος[?], "the wife and the virgin are divided"; the Latin is more correct: "He who is with a wife is anxious for the things of this world and is divided."

units.la: R. Non repugnat Græcus textus versioni Latinæ, & utut legas, eadem est sententia. Sensus textus latini est. Vir conjugatus, non totus totus Deo servit, sed divisus est & externis actionibus distinctus. Sic Græci textus sensus est: Divisa est uxor & virgo, nimirum non naturâ, sed studiis & actionibus; alia enim est sollicitudo mulieris, alia virginis.
units.tr: A. The Greek text does not conflict with the Latin version, and however you read it, the sense is the same. The sense of the Latin text is this: the married man does not serve God wholly, but is divided and distracted by external activities. So the sense of the Greek text is: the wife and the virgin are divided, namely not by nature but by their concerns and activities; for the anxiety of a wife is one thing, that of a virgin another.

units.la: 3. 1.Cor.15. legendum est, Primus homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo de cœlo cœlestis, ut non solùm nostra latina habet, sed etiam Calvinus probat. At Græci constanter legunt, ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος[?] χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος[?] ἐξ οὐρανοῦ[?]. Quam depravationem manifeste patet vitio scriptorum, ex corruptionibus Manichæis.
units.tr: 3. In 1 Corinthians 15, it must be read, "The first man is of the earth, earthly; the second man is of heaven, heavenly," as not only our Latin has it but Calvin also approves. But the Greeks constantly read ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος[?] χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος[?] ἐξ οὐρανοῦ[?]. That this corruption is plainly due to the fault of the scribes, it is clear from the Manichaean corruptions.

units.la: R. Græcus textus nec Marcionitis favet, quasi corpus Christus de cœlo attulerit; nec à Latina quoad sensum discrepat: nec hoc agit Calvinus, l.2.Inst.c.12.&13.& l.4.c.17. ut græcum textum mutet, sed ut eum recte interpretetur. Optimè sanè respondent omnia membra, si essentiæ & qualitatum antithesin talem instituamus: ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος (κατ' οὐσίαν) ἐκ γῆς (κατὰ ποιότητα) χοϊκός: ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος (κατ' οὐσίαν) ὁ κύριος, (κατὰ ποιότητα) ἐξ οὐρανοῦ.
units.tr: A. The Greek text favours neither the Marcionites, as if Christ had brought his body from heaven, nor does it differ from the Latin in sense; nor does Calvin, in Institutes book 2, chapters 12 and 13, and book 4, chapter 17, aim to change the Greek text but to interpret it correctly. Indeed all the members answer very well if we set up the antithesis of essence and quality thus: ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος (κατ' οὐσίαν) ἐκ γῆς (κατὰ ποιότητα) χοϊκός: ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος (κατ' οὐσίαν) ὁ κύριος, (κατὰ ποιότητα) ἐξ οὐρανοῦ.

units.la: 4. Desunt multa in multis exemplaribus, ut Joh.8.historia adulterae: Marci caput ultimum: & testimonium pulcerrimum Trinitatis 1.Joh.5.8.
units.tr: 4. Many things are lacking in many copies, such as the story of the adulteress in John 8, the last chapter of Mark, and the most beautiful testimony of the Trinity in 1 John 5:8.

units.la: R. Fatendum, Novatianorum & Catharorum fraude, duo priora ex multis exemplaribus fuisse expuncta, & tertium Arrianorum perfidiâ. Sed malè ex aliquot particularibus universale colligitur.
units.tr: A. It must be granted that by the fraud of the Novatians and Cathars the first two were expunged from many copies, and the third by the treachery of the Arians. But it is wrongly inferred a universal conclusion from a few particular instances.

units.la: 5. Matth.6. Quia tuum est regnum,&c. Hæc verba non sunt de textu, sed addita à Græcis esse liquet. Primò, quia Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Ambrosius, Hieronymus & Augustinus, in explicatione Orat.Dom.ejus non meminerunt, tum quia Græci hæc verba in liturgia sua recitant, tametsi Orationem Dom. ibi non continuent.
units.tr: 5. Matthew 6: "For thine is the kingdom, etc." It is clear that these words are not from the text but were added by the Greeks. First, because Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine make no mention of them in their explanations of the Lord's Prayer; second, because the Greeks recite these words in their liturgy, although there they do not continue the Lord's Prayer.

units.la: R. 1. Falsò asseritur à Græcis hæc addita, nec ex particularibus aliquot versionibus universale quid colligitur. 2. Verba hæc habet Syrus: habet Chrysostomus: habet Theophylactus & Græci alii, quorum non minor autoritas, quàm Latinorum. 3. Liturgiam illam Græcorum ipsi Papistæ improbant, unde quæ vis argumenti sit, facilè colligitur. Et infirma planè est argumentatio: In liturgia hæc verba, sine Oratione Dominica recitantur: ergo ad Orationem Dominicam non pertinent.
units.tr: A. 1. It is falsely asserted by the Greeks that these were added, and no universal conclusion is drawn from a few particular versions. 2. The Syriac has these words; Chrysostom has them; Theophylact and other Greeks have them, whose authority is no less than that of the Latins. 3. The Papists themselves reject that Greek liturgy, so it is easily gathered what force the argument has. And the argument is plainly weak: in the liturgy these words are recited without the Lord's Prayer; therefore they do not belong to the Lord's Prayer.

units.la: 2. Pro Vulgata Latina.
units.tr: 2. For the Latin Vulgate.

units.la: Argumenta Pontificiorum, pro Latina Vulgata editione petuntur, 1. Ab antiquitate, quia in Ecclesia ante mille trecentos annos usurpata sit. 2. Ab autoritate Patrum illam probantium. 3. Ab æquitate; cùm enim Hebræi suum & Græci suum authenticum textū habeant, etiam latinæ Ecclesiæ suum concedendum, inprimis cùm tres hæ linguæ, in cruce sint sanctificatæ. 4. A necessitate; tum quia multi Hebraicâ & Græcam non calleant; tum quia infinita licentia transferendi oriretur, nisi Latina pro authentica reciperetur.
units.tr: The arguments of the Papists for the Latin edition, the Vulgate, are drawn: 1. From antiquity, since it was used in the Church some thirteen hundred years ago. 2. From the authority of the Fathers who approved it. 3. From fairness: since the Hebrews have their own authentic text and the Greeks theirs, the Latin Church too should be granted its own; especially since these three languages were sanctified on the cross. 4. From necessity: partly because many do not know Hebrew and Greek, and partly because an unlimited freedom of translating would arise unless the Latin were received as authentic.

units.la: R. Infirmiora sunt hæc argumenta, quàm ut longâ refutatione egeant. Ad primum & secundum respondetur, nec unius Eccle-siæ judicio, nec Patrum authoritate nitendum, facileque hoc in negotio authoritatem authoritati opponi. Ad tertium, fallaciam esse, 1. Consequentis: Hebraea & Græca est authentica. Ergo & Latina. 2. A non causa ut causa; ideò enim his linguis titulus ille I. N. R. I. cruci affixus est, ut Hebræi, Græci & Latini illum legerent, & ut significaretur, his linguis Christum prædicandum. Nec sequeretur, Latinâ authentica opus est. Ergo illa erit Vulgata Latina. Ad 4. resp. nullam planè Consequentiâ esse; tum quia ignari, Pastores linguarum peritos consulere; tum quia Ecclesiæ licentiam illam facilè refraenare possunt.
units.tr: Answer: These arguments are too weak to need a lengthy refutation. To the first and second it is replied that we must rest neither on the judgement of one Church nor on the authority of the Fathers, and that in this matter authority is easily set against authority. To the third, it is a fallacy: (1) of the consequent: the Hebrew and Greek are authentic, therefore the Latin is too. (2) Of a non-cause taken as a cause: that title I.N.R.I. was fixed to the cross in those languages so that Hebrews, Greeks and Latins might read it, and to signify that Christ is to be preached in these languages; and it would not follow that an authentic Latin is needed, so that it would be the Latin Vulgate. To the fourth, the reply is that there is plainly no consequence: partly because the ignorant consult the ministers, who are skilled in the languages; partly because they can easily restrain that licence of the Church.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA. In qua DE S. SCRIPTVRÆ PERFECTIONE.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO TERTIA. In which concerning the PERFECTION OF HOLY SCRIPTURE.

units.la: Status Controversiæ.
units.tr: The State of the Controversy.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: SACRAM Scripturam seu Verbum Dei ἔγγραφον[?] fidei principium esse, nemo Christianus negaverit.
units.tr: No Christian would deny that Holy Scripture, or the written Word of God, is the principle of faith.

units.la: 2. Hoc verò quæritur, inter nos & Pontificios, An unicum fidei principium sit, & sic perfectum, ut ad salutem sufficiat?
units.tr: 2. The question between us and the Papists, however, is this: is it the sole principle of faith, and so perfect that it suffices for salvation?

units.la: 3. Pontificii negant, & præter Verbum Dei scriptum, verbum quoq; ἄγγραφον[?] commīniscuntur,& traditiones extra Scripturas, tanquam ad salutem necessarias, obtrudunt. Bell.l.4.de Verbo Dei,c.3.
units.tr: 3. The Papists deny this. Besides the written Word of God, they invent an unwritten word as well, and they press upon us traditions outside the Scriptures as necessary to salvation. Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 4, chapter 3.

units.la: 4. Nos etsi fateamur, non omnes traditiones repudiandas esse, inprimis illas, quæ de rebus adiaphoris,& ad externum tantùm Ecclesiæ ritum pertinentibus, sonant: negamus tamen, ullam traditionem, extra Scripturas, simpliciter ad salutem necessariam esse.
units.tr: 4. We grant that not all traditions are to be rejected, especially those that concern indifferent matters and pertain only to the external rite of the Church. We deny, however, that any tradition outside the Scriptures is simply necessary to salvation.

units.la: 5. Imò confidenter afferimus, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, in Scripturis contineri omnia, eamq; credentibus ad salutem sufficere.
units.tr: 5. Indeed, we confidently affirm that everything necessary to salvation is contained in the Scriptures, and that for those who believe them they are sufficient for salvation.

units.la: Confirmatio nostræ sententiæ.
units.tr: Confirmation of our Position.

units.la: Sententia nostra stabilitur,
units.tr: Our position is established:

units.la: 1. Expresis testimoniis, quibus Scriptura nobis tanquam fidei & vitæ regula perfecta commendatur. Psal.19.v.8.9. Lex Domini perfecta,&c. Joh.20.31. Hæc scripta sunt, ut credatis Jesum esse Christum, Filium Dei, & credentes vitam habeatis, per nomen ejus. 2.Tim.3.v.15. Teq; à puero sacras literas novisse, qua te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem,&c.
units.tr: 1. By express testimonies, in which Scripture is commended to us as the perfect rule of faith and life. Psalm 19:8-9, "The law of the Lord is perfect," etc. John 20:31, "These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name." 2 Timothy 3:15, "and that from childhood you have known the sacred letters, which can make you wise unto salvation," etc.

units.la: II. Rationibus.
units.tr: II. By Arguments.

units.la: 1. Quia Canoni Scripturarum nec addendum, nec detrahendum. Deut.4.2.&5.38.&12.32. Apoc.22.18.19.
units.tr: 1. Because nothing is to be added to the canon of Scripture, nor taken away from it. Deuteronomy 4:2, 5:38, 12:32; Revelation 22:18-19.

units.la: 2. Quia in rebus Religionis, ad Scripturam ablegamur: Esaiae 8.20. ad legem & testimonium. Luc.16.29. Habent Mosen & Prophetas. Joh.5.39. Scrutamini Scripturas.
units.tr: 2. Because in matters of religion we are sent back to Scripture: Isaiah 8:20, "to the law and the testimony." Luke 16:29, "They have Moses and the Prophets." John 5:39, "Search the Scriptures."

units.la: 3. Si non omnia complectitur Spiritus S. in Scripturis, aut ideo illud factum, quod non potuerit, aut quod noluerit id facere. At illud naturae divinae; hoc officio, scopo & amori Spiritus S. erga fideles repugnat.
units.tr: 3. If the Holy Spirit has not comprised everything in the Scriptures, then either he could not do so, or he would not. But the former is repugnant to the divine nature, and the latter to the office, purpose and love of the Holy Spirit toward the faithful.

units.la: 4. Traditiones illae, quas Pontificii necessarias esse dicunt, aut secundum, aut praeter, aut contra Scripturam erut[?]. Primum traditionis genus, non simpliciter ad salutem necessarium est; si enim secundum Scripturam est, tum in Scripturis contineri necesse est, nec acceptatur, nisi quatenus Scripturis consonat. Secundum vero & tertium genus, Deus ipse aversatur. Esaiae 29.13. Matth.15.9. Gal.1.14. Colos.2.8.22. Nullum igitur traditionis genus extra Scripturas est necessarium.
units.tr: 4. Those traditions which the Papists say are necessary are either according to Scripture, or beside Scripture, or against Scripture. The first kind of tradition is not simply necessary to salvation: for if it is according to Scripture, then it must of necessity be contained in the Scriptures, and it is accepted only in so far as it agrees with the Scriptures. The second and third kinds, however, God himself rejects: Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:9; Galatians 1:14; Colossians 2:8, 22. No kind of tradition outside the Scriptures is therefore necessary.

units.la: Assertio nostrae sententiae contra Pon- tificiorum objectiones.
units.tr: The Assertion of our Position against the Objections of the Papists.

units.la: Pontificii, ut ipsis sub traditionum ad salutem necessariarum specie quidlibet fingere liceat, pro illarum necessitate & Scripturae insufficientia, strenue militant. Praecipuas igitur ipsorum objectiones paucis diluamus.
units.tr: The Papists, so that they may be free to invent whatever they like under the guise of traditions necessary to salvation, fight vigorously for their necessity and for the insufficiency of Scripture. We will therefore briefly refute their principal objections.

units.la: 1. Si nec Christus librum quempiam scripsit, nec Apostoli ejus mandato scripserunt, cum verbum ἐγγράφον[?] unicum & persectum fidei principium non est. Prius est. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: 1. If neither Christ wrote any book nor his Apostles wrote at his command, then the written word is not the sole and perfect principle of faith. The first is true. Therefore so is the second.

units.la: R. Falsum est Assumtum: tum quia Christus, tanquam Caput, Ministerio Apostolorum, tanquam manuum, scripsit: tum quia mandatum ejus rei a Christo acceperunt; missi enim sunt ad docendum. Matth.cap.10. & 28. Atqui docendi ratio duplex est; aut enim viva voce, aut scriptis docemus. Quod vero scriptis quoque doceri voluerit, testimonia sunt evidentissima; Nam 2.Tim.3.16. Tota Scriptura divinitus inspirata, dicitur, & Apoc.1.v.11. Johannes expresse scribere jubetur.
units.tr: Answer: The assumption is false, both because Christ, as Head, wrote through the ministry of the Apostles as his hands, and because they received a command from Christ to do so; for they were sent to teach: Matthew chapters 10 and 28. Now there are two ways of teaching: we teach either by the living voice or by writing. That he also wished to be taught in writing, the testimonies are most evident; for 2 Timothy 3:16 says that all Scripture is divinely inspired, and in Revelation 1:11 John is expressly commanded to write.

units.la: 2. Si Christus Discipulis suis ante resurrectionem non omnia dixit, nec, quae post resurrectionem cum ipsis communicavit, scripta extant, tum Scriptura ad salutem non erit suffi-ciens. ciens. Prius est, Johan. 16[?].v.12.13. Adhuc multa habeo, &c. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: 2. If Christ did not tell his disciples everything before the resurrection, and the things he communicated to them after the resurrection are not extant in writing, then Scripture will not be sufficient for salvation. The first is true: John 16:12-13, "I still have many things to say," etc. Therefore so is the second.

units.la: R. Committitur duplex fallacia Accidentis; nec enim verba illa, Adhuc multa habeo, de rerum credendarum substantia, sed de illustriori patefaciendi modo intelliguntur; dubium enim non est, quin res necessariae ad salutem, Discipulis, etiam ante resurrectionem, patefactae sint: rursus, quae Christus Discipulis post resurrectionem revelavit, tametsi totidem literis & syllabis scripta non sint; quoad substantiam tamen, fidelissime consignata sunt, cum in Historia Euangelica, tum in Epistolis & in Apocalypsi. Unde merito exclamat Johannes 1.ep.1.1. Quod vidimus, quod audivimus, &c.
units.tr: Answer: Two fallacies of accident are committed here. For those words, "I still have many things to say," are understood not of the substance of the things to be believed, but of a more illustrious mode of revealing them. For there is no doubt that the things necessary to salvation were revealed to the disciples even before the resurrection. Again, what Christ revealed to the disciples after the resurrection, although it is not written down in exactly the same letters and syllables, has nevertheless been most faithfully recorded in substance, both in the Gospel history and in the Epistles and in the Apocalypse. Whence John rightly exclaims, 1 John 1:1, "What we have seen, what we have heard," etc.

units.la: 3. Traditiones ab ipsis Apostolis commendantur 1.Cor.11.2. 2.Thess.2.15. 1.Tim.6.20. & 2.Tim.1.14. & 2.2. Ergo necessariae sunt.
units.tr: 3. Traditions are commended by the Apostles themselves: 1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 6:20; 2 Timothy 1:14; and 2 John. Therefore they are necessary.

units.la: R. Luditur fallacia Homonymiae: in Conclusione enim intelliguntur traditiones, non scriptae, ad salutem simpliciter necessariae. At in Antecedente vox Traditionis sumitur, aut pro doctrina divina, scriptis ab Apostolis tradita, ut 2.Thess.2.15. 1.Tim.6.20. 2.Tim.1.14. & 2.2. Aut pro constitutione libera, ritum tantum Ecclesiasticum concernente. 1.Cor.11.2.
units.tr: Answer: A fallacy of equivocation is played here. In the conclusion, traditions are understood as unwritten traditions simply necessary to salvation. But in the antecedent the word tradition is taken either for divine teaching handed down by the Apostles in writing, as in 2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 6:20; 2 Timothy 1:14; and 2 John; or for a free ordinance concerning only the ecclesiastical rite, as in 1 Corinthians 11:2.

units.la: 4. Multa dogmata ad salutem necessaria in Scripturis non reperiuntur; nusquam enim in illis occurrit, Trinitas, Persona, ὁμοούσιον[?], & similes voces. Nihil, de medio, quo foeminae olim purgatae sunt a peccato originali, cum masculi solum fuerint circumcisi. Nihil de morientibus ante circumcisione. Nihil de S. Coena nemini danda, nisi post Baptismum. Nihil de paedobaptismo, de die Dominico, de symbolo Apostolico, de assumtione corporis beatae Virginis, ejusque perpetua Virginitate, de dignoscendis libris Canonicis. Ergo Scriptura ad salutem non est sufficiens.
units.tr: 4. Many dogmas necessary to salvation are not found in the Scriptures; for nowhere in them does the word Trinity, Person, homoousios, or similar terms occur. Nothing is said, concerning the means by which women were formerly purged of original sin, since only males were circumcised. Nothing is said of those who died before circumcision. Nothing of the Lord's Supper being given to no one except after baptism. Nothing of infant baptism, of the Lord's Day, of the Apostles' Creed, of the assumption of the body of the blessed Virgin, and of her perpetual virginity, or of distinguishing the canonical books. Therefore Scripture is not sufficient for salvation.

units.la: R. Duplex hic fallacia notanda; altera plurium Interrogatorum: Accidentis altera. Illa committitur, ea congerendo, quorum neutiquam eadem est ratio; alia enim ad salutem non necessaria sunt, ut dogma de perpetua Mariae virginitate, etsi illud pie credamus: alia conficta sunt, ut fabula de assumtione corporis ipsius: alia necessaria quidem sunt, sed in Scripturis aut express√® traduntur, aut exinde per bonam consequentiam colliguntur. e.g. De voce Trinitatis, Personæ & ὁμοούσιᾳ[?] frustra litigatur, cùm res ipsa in Scripturis clarissimè doceatur. Circumcisio in V.T. non minùs fœmellis, quàm masculis profuit, quia in masculis, tanquam prototypis, illæ quoque sunt sanctificatæ; nam ad filias æquè ac filios pertinebat illa promissio Gen.17.14. Ero Deus tuus & feminis tui. Ut jam nihil dicatur de falsa opinione, operis operati, quasi externa circumcisio à peccatis purgasset: ex qua & alter scrupulus ortus est, de morientibus ante circumcisionem, cui eximendo sufficit, quòd Abrahamus, jam ante circumcisionem justificatus dicitur. Rom.4.10. Jus S.Cœnæ participandæ, nondum baptizatis, derogat tùm analogia Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti; quia incircumcisis non licebat Pascha comedere: tùm natura Baptismi & S.Cœnæ; naturâ enim & tempore prius esse debet Sacramentum regenerationis, quàm Sacramentum refectionis, sicut prior est nativitas, quàm nutritio. Pædobaptismum satis evincit analogia Baptismi & circumcisionis, nec non fœderis divini promissiones, quæ infantibus non minùs, quàm adultis factæ. Nec verò quicquam absurdius est, quàm illis negare signum cœlestis heredita-tis, quibus Christus Regnum cœlorum adjudicat. Matth.19.14. Quibus & illud accedit, quòd Apostoli integras familias baptizasse leguntur. Diei Dominicæ sanctificatio abunde ex Actor.20.7. 1.Cor.16.2. & Apoc.1.10. probatur: Symbolum verò Apostolicum, cùm nihil aliud, quàm scriptorum Apostolicorum medulla sit, quis in Scripturis contineri negaverit? De libris tandem Canonicis, ex ipsis Scripturis optimè judicari, suprà ostensum est.
units.tr: Answer: Two fallacies are to be noted here: the first is that of many questions, the second that of accident. The first is committed by heaping together things which by no means have the same reason. For some are not necessary to salvation, such as the dogma of Mary's perpetual virginity, though we piously believe it; others are invented, such as the fable of the assumption of her body itself; others indeed are necessary, but are either expressly delivered in the Scriptures, or are gathered from them by good consequence. For example, the words Trinity, Person and homoousios are contended over in vain, since the thing itself is taught most clearly in the Scriptures. Circumcision in the Old Testament benefited females no less than males, since in males, as prototypes, the females also were sanctified; for that promise, Genesis 17:14, "I will be God to you and to your seed," pertained to daughters equally as to sons. Not to mention the false opinion of the work done, as if external circumcision purged from sins: out of which also the other scruple arose, concerning those who died before circumcision, which is removed sufficiently by the fact that Abraham is said to have been justified even before circumcision, Romans 4:10. The right to partake of the Lord's Supper before being baptized is contrary both to the analogy of the Sacraments of the Old Testament, since the uncircumcised were not permitted to eat the Passover, and to the nature of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; for the sacrament of regeneration must be prior both in nature and in time to the sacrament of refreshment, just as birth is prior to nourishment. Infant baptism is sufficiently proven by the analogy of Baptism and circumcision, and also by the promises of the divine covenant, which were made to infants no less than to adults. Indeed nothing is more absurd than to deny the sign of heavenly inheritance to those to whom Christ adjudges the kingdom of heaven, Matthew 19:14. To which is added that the Apostles are read to have baptized whole households. The sanctification of the Lord's Day is abundantly proven from Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2 and Revelation 1:10. As for the Apostles' Creed, since it is nothing other than the marrow of the Apostolic writings, who would deny that it is contained in the Scriptures? Concerning the canonical books, finally, it has been shown above that they are best judged from the Scriptures themselves.

units.la: 5. Si Scriptura perfecta est, aut totus Canon, aut singuli libri perfecti erunt. Non totus canon, quia multi libri perierunt; ex Veteri Testamento plures, ut ex Josuæ 10.v.12. 1.Reg. 14.v.19. & aliis locis apparet. Ex N.Testamento, inprimis epistola ad Laodicenses, de qua Colofs.4.v.ult. Non singuli libri; si enim unus perfectus foret, reliqui non essent necessarii.
units.tr: 5. If Scripture is perfect, then either the whole canon or the individual books will be perfect. Not the whole canon, because many books have perished; of the Old Testament, several, as appears from Joshua 10:12, 1 Kings 14:19 and other places. Of the New Testament, above all the epistle to the Laodiceans, concerning which see Colossians 4:16 (last verse). Not the individual books; for if one were perfect, the others would not be necessary.

units.la: R. 1. Ad dilemmatis propositionem. Alia perfectio essentialis, alia integralis est. Essentialis perfectio Scripturæ, in divina ejus materia & forma consistit, hac ratione & totus Canon & singuli libri perfecti sunt. Integralis vero perfectio in doctrinae ad salutem sufficientia sita est, & hac ratione non solum totus Canon, sed & quidam libri perfecti sunt. 2. Ad assumti prius lemma. Negamus ullū librum S.Scripturae periisse. Veteris Testamenti testimonia, non de libris divinis, sed de annalibus, in publicum usum collectis, sunt intelligenda. Testimonium vero ex N.T.citatum, corruptum est, nec enim ad Laodicenses, sed ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ[?] scripsit Apostolus, & haec epistola, Theophylacti judicio, est prior ad Timotheum, vide 1.Tim.6.v.ult. 3. Ad posterius lemma. Dicimus falsam esse probationis illius consequentiam. Singuli libri sunt perfecti, ergo reliquis non opus erat; Etsi enim Epistola ad Romanos, vel alia quaepiam Scripturae pars, res ad salutem necessarias perfecte tradat, non tamen ideo reliqui libri, ad uberiorem declarationem & confirmationem, non erunt necessarii.
units.tr: 1. To the proposition of the dilemma: there is one perfection that is essential and another that is integral. The essential perfection of Scripture consists in its divine matter and form; on this ground both the whole canon and the individual books are perfect. Integral perfection, however, lies in the sufficiency of the teaching for salvation, and on this ground not only the whole canon but also certain individual books are perfect. 2. To the assumed prior lemma: we deny that any book of Holy Scripture has perished. The testimonies of the Old Testament are to be understood not of the divine books but of the annals, collected for public use. The testimony cited from the New Testament is corrupted: the Apostle did not write "to the Laodiceans" but [ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ?], and this epistle, in the judgment of Theophylact, is the earlier one to Timothy; see 1 Tim. 6, last verse. 3. To the posterior lemma: we say that the consequence of that proof is false. "The individual books are perfect, therefore the others were not needed." For even if the Epistle to the Romans, or some other part of Scripture, delivers perfectly the things necessary to salvation, the other books will nonetheless not be unnecessary for a fuller declaration and confirmation.

units.la: 6. Quaevis Respublica regitur jure scripto & non scripto. Ergo & Ecclesia traditionibus non scriptis regitur.
units.tr: 6. Every commonwealth is governed by written and unwritten law. Therefore the Church too is governed by unwritten traditions.

units.la: R. Negatur Consequentia; impar enim ratio est, Ecclesiae & Reipublicae; Respublicae enim divino & humano jure reguntur, Ecclesia non nisi divino & scripto.
units.tr: To this we reply: the consequence is denied. The reason is not equal in the case of the Church and of the commonwealth. For commonwealths are governed by divine and human law, whereas the Church is governed by divine and written law only.

units.la: DISPUTATIO QUARTA. In qua DE USU SCRIPTURÆ COMMUNI ET PUBLICO.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO QUARTA. In which the common and public use of Scripture is discussed.

units.la: Status Controversiæ.
units.tr: The State of the Controversy.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: CONTROVERSIÆ, quas de Scriptura movent Pontificii, eò unicè collimant, ut pro limpidissimis ejus sontibus, fœdas traditionum lacunas, nobis obtrudant.
units.tr: The controversies that the Papists raise concerning Scripture aim solely at this: that, while the purest springs of it are at hand, they force upon us the foul gaps left by tradition.

units.la: 2. Hoc sine[?], Scripturae autoritatem elevant, libros Apocryphos cum Canonicis commiscent, & pro Scripturæ imperfectione, tanquam pro aris & focis pugnant.
units.tr: 2. By this (sine[?]) they lower the authority of Scripture, mix the Apocryphal books with the canonical ones, and fight over the imperfection of Scripture as if for their altars and hearths.

units.la: 3. Eandem ob caussam, communem & promiscuum, Scripturæ, in lingua cuique genti vernacula, usum & lectionem, miseræ plebeculæ, eripere omnibus modis satagunt.
units.tr: 3. For the same reason they labour by every means to snatch from the poor common folk the common and promiscuous use and reading of Scripture in the vernacular tongue of each nation.

units.la: 4. In hac autem Controversia, tres Quæsti[?]nes, distinctè considerandæ sunt.
units.tr: 4. In this controversy, three questions are to be considered distinctly.

units.la: I. An ea sit Scriptura perspicuitas, ut à quibusvis Christianis cum fructu legi possit?
units.tr: I. Is Scripture so clear that it can be read with profit by any Christians whatever?

units.la: II. An in lingua cuiq[?]genti vernacula, à quibusvis legi debeat?
units.tr: II. Ought it to be read by anyone whatever in the vernacular tongue of each nation?

units.la: III. An preces & sacra publica, vernaculâ linguâ, per agi oporteat?
units.tr: III. Ought prayers and public worship to be conducted in the vernacular tongue?

units.la: De Prima Quæstione.
units.tr: On the First Question.

units.la: 1. Pontificii Scripturas obscuriores esse contendunt, quàm ut à Laicis legi aut intelligi queant. Bell.I.2.de V.D.c.16.
units.tr: 1. The Papists contend that the Scriptures are too obscure to be read or understood by laymen. Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 1, chapter 16.

units.la: 2. Nos verò, tametsi multa in Scripturis intellectu difficilia esse, ultrò fateamur; hoc tamen affirmamus, Scripturam laicis quoque, eam piè & cum divini Numinis implorationè, legentibus, in rebus ad salutem necessariis, perspicuam esse.
units.tr: 2. We, however, while readily admitting that many things in Scripture are difficult to understand, affirm this: that Scripture is clear, even to laymen, in those matters necessary to salvation, for those who read it piously and with prayer to the divine Majesty for help.

units.la: Confirmatio nostræ sententiæ.
units.tr: Confirmation of our position.

units.la: I. Testimonia de perspicuitate Scripturæ clarissima sunt. Deut.30.11. Præceptum, quod ego tibi præcipio hodie, non est occultum à te, neq; longinquum. Psal.19.9. Præceptum Jehovæ purum est, illuminans oculos. Psal.119.105. Verbum tuum, lucerna pedibus meis. 2.Cor.4.3. Si tectum est nostrum Euangelium, iis tectum est, qui pereunt.
units.tr: I. The testimonies concerning the clarity of Scripture are most plain. Deut. 30.11: The commandment which I command you this day is not hidden from you, nor is it far off. Ps. 19.9: The commandment of Jehovah is pure, enlightening the eyes. Ps. 119.105: Your word is a lamp to my feet. 2 Cor. 4.3: If our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.

units.la: II. Accedunt sequentes rationes.
units.tr: II. The following reasons are added.

units.la: 1. Quia nullum caput Religionis est, quod in illa non perspicuè traditur, ut omnium inductione facilè probari posset.
units.tr: 1. Because there is no chief article of religion which is not plainly taught in it, so that this could easily be proved by an induction of all of them.

units.la: 2. Quia uno loco obscurior, altero clarior est & se ipsam explicat.
units.tr: 2. Because what is obscure in one place is clearer in another, and it explains itself.

units.la: 3. Quia Spiritus S. negotium salutis in Scripturis clarè docere aut non potuisset, aut noluisset. Neutrum verò citra blasphemiam, de Spiritu S. pronunciari posset.
units.tr: 3. Because the Holy Spirit either could not, or would not, clearly teach the business of salvation in Scripture. Yet neither of these could be asserted concerning the Holy Spirit without blasphemy.

units.la: III. Dignissima verò sunt hæc Patrum testimonia, quæ aspergantur. Cyrill. Alexandr. cont. Julianum l.7. Scripturæ omnibus sunt nota, parvis & magnis, nullius [nempe in necessariis] captum transcendunt. Isidor.l.2.epist.5. Deus non tantum dignitatis suæ rationem habuit, in edendis Scripturis, sed rudibus & incultis verbis, cœlestes disciplinas temperavit, ut mulier, puer, & omnium indoctissimus, aliquid commodi perciperet, gregalium hominum saluti benignè prospiciens, neminem suâ utilitate privans. August. de doctr. Christ. cap. 6. Ita Spiritus sanctus, magnificè & salubriter Scripturas sanctas modificavit, ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret, obscurioribus autem fastidia detergeret, nihil enim ferè de istis obscurioribus eruitur, quod non planissimè alibi reperiatur.
units.tr: III. Indeed, these testimonies of the Fathers, which may be cited, are most worthy. Cyril of Alexandria, against Julian, book 7: The Scriptures are known to all, small and great alike; they surpass the grasp of no one [namely in necessary matters]. Isidore, book 2, letter 5: God not only had regard for his own dignity in publishing the Scriptures, but tempered the heavenly teachings in rude and unpolished words, so that a woman, a boy, and the most unlearned of all might gain some benefit, kindly providing for the salvation of ordinary men and depriving no one of his usefulness. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, chapter 6: Thus the Holy Spirit so magnificently and wholesomely tempered the holy Scriptures that he met hunger in the more open passages, and removed disgust in the more obscure ones, for almost nothing is drawn out of those obscure passages that is not found most plainly elsewhere.

units.la: Assertio sententiae nostrae contra Pon- tificiorum objectiones.
units.tr: Assertion of our opinion against the objections of the Papists.

units.la: Rationes Pontificiorum pro obscuritate Scripturæ, ipsæ quoque obscuræ, elumbes & infirmæ, sunt sequentes. I. Quia David aliique sancti Verbum Dei sibi revelari petant. Psal.119.18. II. Quia Emmauntem euntibus explicanda fuit. Luc.24. III. Quia Scriptura lux in tenebris lucens dicitur.2.Pet.1.v.19. IV. Quia in Pauli scriptis nonnulla obscura esse, testatur Petrus.2.Pet.3.16. V. Quia & res & modus tradendi, captum laicorum excedunt: res enim quod attinet, sunt illæ sublimes, ut SS.Trinitatis Mysterium & similia: modus verò docendi, involutus est tropis, figuris, sententiis ambiguis & crypticis. VI. Patres quoq; de obscuritate Scripturarū passim testantur.
units.tr: The arguments of the Papists for the obscurity of Scripture are themselves obscure, feeble and weak. They are as follows. I. Because David and other saints ask that the Word of God be revealed to them. Ps. 119:18. II. Because the disciples going to Emmaus had to have Scripture explained to them. Luke 24. III. Because Scripture is said to be a light shining in a dark place. 2 Pet. 1:19. IV. Because Peter testifies that some things in Paul's writings are hard to understand. 2 Pet. 3:16. V. Because both the subject matter and the manner of teaching exceed the grasp of the laity: as to the subject matter, it is lofty, such as the mystery of the Holy Trinity and similar things; as to the manner of teaching, it is wrapped in tropes, figures, ambiguous and cryptic sayings. VI. The Fathers too testify everywhere to the obscurity of the Scriptures.
