units.la: R. Nulla ferè istarum rationum est, in qua non committatur Elenchi Ignoratio. Nec enim asserimus, ita perspicuam esse Scripturam, ut nihil in illa occurrat difficultatis, nec precibus, legendi assiduitate & similibus mediis opus sit. Interim non obstant hæ objectiones, quin maneat, necessaria Religionis capita, in Scripturis clarissimè tradi. Testimonia Petri, pro nobis potiùs faciunt. Si enim Scriptura lux in tenebris lucens est, non igitur obscura est. Rursus, Si nonnulla tantùm in Pauli scripturis obscura sunt, ergo pleraque sunt clara & manifesta.
units.tr: Reply: Almost none of these arguments avoids the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi. For we do not assert that Scripture is so plain that nothing in it presents any difficulty, nor that prayer, constant reading and similar means are unnecessary. Meanwhile these objections do not prevent it from remaining that the necessary heads of religion are set out most clearly in the Scriptures. The testimony of Peter rather favours us. For if Scripture is a light shining in a dark place, then it is not obscure. Again, if only some things in Paul's writings are obscure, then most things are clear and manifest.

units.la: SECUNDA QUÆSTIO.
units.tr: SECOND QUESTION.

units.la: 1. Papistæ Scripturæ, in lingua vernacula, lectionem Laicis permittendam negant: exceptis illis tantùm, qui ejus rei copiam ab Episcopo aut ab Inquisitore peculiariter impetrarunt.
units.tr: 1. The Papists deny that the reading of Scripture in the vernacular should be permitted to the laity, except for those only who have obtained a special licence to do so from the bishop or the Inquisitor.

units.la: 2. Nos verò cōmunem Scripturae,in lingua vernaculâ,usum & lectionem etiam laicis permittendum,firmiter statuimus.
units.tr: 2. But we firmly maintain that the common use and reading of Scripture in the vernacular should be permitted even to the laity.

units.la: Nostræ sententiæ confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation of our opinion.

units.la: I. Probatur illa expresis Dei mandatis, quibus omnibus, etiam indoctis ac plebeis, Scripturae lectionem mandat. Deut.6.9. Inscribito ea postibus domus tuae,&c. Et 17.19. Esto exemplar legis penes Regem. Joh.5.39. Scrutamini Scripturas. Colos.3.16. Sermo Christi habitet in vobis copiosè,&c. Apoc.1. Beatus qui hac legit & intelligit.
units.tr: I. This is proved by the express commands of God, by which he commands the reading of Scripture to all, even the unlearned and common people. Deut. 6:9. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house, etc. And 17:19. Let it be a copy of the law kept by the King. John 5:39. Search the Scriptures. Col. 3:16. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, etc. Rev. 1. Blessed is he who reads and understands these things.

units.la: II. Id ipsum confirmant Euangeliorum & Epistolarum inscriptiones; Lucas enim Euangelii utramque partem inscribit Theophilo, Paulus omnibus fidelibus, qui Romae, Corinthi & aliis locis erant. Johannes verò diser tisimè inquit, Scribo vobis,patres,adolescentes,pueruli,& c. 1.Joh.2.13.
units.tr: II. The inscriptions of the Gospels and Epistles confirm the same: Luke dedicates both parts of his Gospel to Theophilus, Paul addresses all the faithful who were at Rome, Corinth and other places. John indeed very clearly says, I write to you, fathers, young men, little children, etc. 1 John 2:13.

units.la: III. In promtu quoq; sunt istiusmodi lectionis exempla. In Æthiope Act.8. in Beroënsibus Act.17.11. & in Ecclesiis,ad quas scripsit Petrus 2.ep.1.19.
units.tr: III. Examples of such reading are also ready to hand: in the Ethiopian, Acts 8; in the Bereans, Acts 17:11; and in the churches to which Peter wrote, 2 Pet. 1:19.

units.la: IV. Denique Patres quoque assentiuntur.
units.tr: IV. Finally, the Fathers also agree.

units.la: Origenes in Matth.4. Scripturae sunt fons Jacob: siquidem in Scripturis bibunt docti,ut Jacob & filii,& indocti,ut pecora ejus.
units.tr: Origen on Matthew, book 4: The Scriptures are the well of Jacob: for in the Scriptures the learned drink, as Jacob and his sons did, and the unlearned, as his flocks did.

units.la: Gregor.Nazianz. hom.4. Dom.Epiph. Hanc consuetudinem Christiani habere debent, ut quotidie ad Ecclesiam veniant, & legant ipsi,si non valent,audiant legentes.
units.tr: Gregory of Nazianzus, homily 4, on the Day of Epiphany: Christians ought to have this custom, that they come to the Church every day and read for themselves; if they are not able, let them hear those who read.

units.la: Hier.in Ps.86. Plato scripsit non populo,sed paucis: at Christus Dominus per Apostolos,non paucis,sed universo populo.
units.tr: Jerome on Psalm 86: Plato wrote not for the people but for a few; but the Lord Christ, through the Apostles, wrote not for a few but for the whole people.

units.la: Chrys.hom.2.in Matth. Quotquot estis seculares, comparate vobis Biblia. Dicetis, oves sumus, nostrum est Pastores audire. Oves estis, sed rationales.
units.tr: Chrysostom, homily 2 on Matthew: As many of you as are laymen, get yourselves the Bible. You will say, "We are sheep, it is for our ministers to hear." You are sheep, but rational sheep.

units.la: Isid.l.1.de summo Bono: Scriptura ut Manna, communis perfectis,parvulis & singulis,juxta sensuum suorum capacitatem congruit.
units.tr: Isidore, book 1, On the Highest Good: Scripture, like manna, suits all alike, the perfect and the little ones, each according to the capacity of his senses.

units.la: Greg.Magnus: Scriptura fluvius est,in quo Elephas natare possit, agnus ambulare.
units.tr: Gregory the Great: Scripture is a river in which an elephant may swim and a lamb may walk.

units.la: Assertio nostræ sententiæ contra Pa- pistarum objectiones.
units.tr: Assertion of our opinion against the objections of the Papists.

units.la: 1. Provocant ad praxin Veteris Ecclesiæ. Populus Judaicus, inquiunt, post captivitatē Babylonicā, chaldaicè loquutus est, & tamē Sacrae Literae illi lectae sunt hebraicae; sicut & Christi tempore factum, tametsi nō Hebraea, sed Syra tunc esset vulgaris. Sic Apostoli quoq; variis nationibus nō vernacula cujusq; linguā, sed tantum græcè scripserūt. Et initiò 20.circiter annos, nulla fuit N.Testamenti Scriptura, unde & nulla ejus lectio.
units.tr: 1. They appeal to the practice of the ancient Church. The Jewish people, they say, after the Babylonian captivity spoke Chaldee, and yet the Holy Scriptures were read to them in Hebrew; the same was done at Christ's time, although Hebrew was not then the common tongue but Syriac. So too the Apostles wrote to various nations not in each one's vernacular, but only in Greek. And at the beginning, for about twenty years, there was no Scripture of the New Testament, and therefore no reading of it.

units.la: R. Magna est, in horum exemplorū productione, Accidentis fallacia: primum & secundum quod attinet, non disparatae plane sunt linguae, Hebraea, Chaldaea & Syra, sed Dialectis tantum differentes. Apostolos quod attinet, aliam in scribendo, aliam in docendo tenuerunt rationem: græcè scripserunt; quia tum nulla lingua communior erat, & in quibusvis Regionibus erant, qui græcam callebāt: interim tamen vernaculâ cuique nationi prædicarunt. Novi Testamenti initium quod attinet, etsi tunc nondum scripserint Apostoli, legerunt tamen fideles sermonem propheticum, 2.Petr.1.19. Nec ab Ecclesia nascente ad adultam valet consequentia.
units.tr: Reply: In the production of these examples there is a great fallacy of accident. As to the first and second, the languages Hebrew, Chaldee and Syriac are not plainly different tongues but only differing dialects. As to the Apostles, they followed one method in writing and another in teaching: they wrote in Greek, because at that time no language was more widely shared, and there were people in every region who knew Greek; yet meanwhile they preached to each nation in its own vernacular. As to the beginning of the New Testament, although the Apostles had not yet written, the faithful still read the prophetic word, 2 Pet. 1:19. Nor does the inference hold from the infant Church to the grown one.

units.la: 2. Latina lingua communissima est. Ergo Latina Biblia habere satis est.
units.tr: 2. Latin is the most widely shared language. Therefore it is enough to have the Latin Bible.

units.la: R. Falsum est Antecedens; Latina quippe lingua, literatis inprimis nota est: jam vero multò major est indoctorum numerus, proinde vernaculas versiones habere satius est.
units.tr: Reply: The premise is false; for Latin is known above all to the learned. Indeed the number of the unlearned is far greater, and therefore it is better to have versions in the vernacular.

units.la: 3. Ex S.Scripturae lectione facile haereses oriuntur. Ergo non quibusvis legendae.
units.tr: 3. From the reading of Holy Scripture heresies easily arise. Therefore it should not be read by everyone.

units.la: R. 1. Ad Consequentiam. Abusus rei non tollit usum.
units.tr: Reply: 1. As to the inference: the abuse of a thing does not remove its use.

units.la: 2. Ad Antecedens. Scriptura per se non parit haereses, sed oriuntur illae ex impiorum nefaria detorsione ac depravatione, ut docet Petrus 2.ep.c.3.
units.tr: 2. As to the premise: Scripture of itself does not give birth to heresies; they arise from the wicked distortion and corruption of the impious, as Peter teaches in 2 Pet. 3.

units.la: 4. Si cuique Scriptura vernaculâ linguâ legenda est, singulis fere seculis novas versiones fabricari oportebit.
units.tr: 4. If Scripture is to be read by each person in the vernacular, it will be necessary to make new versions almost every century.

units.la: R. Negatur Consequentia; quia non ita uno seculo variant linguae, quin vetus aliqua versio locum habeat.
units.tr: Reply: The inference is denied; for languages do not change so much in one century that some older version would not still serve.

units.la: 5. Indignum est, inquit Bellarm. Scripturam, opificum, sutorum & fabrorum manibus conteri.
units.tr: 5. It is unworthy, says Bellarmine, for Scripture to be worn down by the hands of workmen, cobblers and smiths.

units.la: R. Indigna homine Christiano sententia: quasi vero Scripturarum lectione indigni sint, pro quibus Christus sanguinem fundere dignatus est.
units.tr: Reply: This opinion is unworthy of a Christian man: as if those for whom Christ deigned to shed his blood were unworthy of reading the Scriptures.

units.la: DE TERTIA QUÆSTIONE.
units.tr: On the Third Question.

units.la: 1. Pontificii docent, non necesse esse, ut preces & alia sacra publica, in Ecclesiis patria cujusque coetus lingua, peragantur.
units.tr: 1. The Papists teach that it is not necessary for prayers and other public sacred rites to be performed in the Churches in the language of each assembly's people.

units.la: 2. Nos id necessarium plane judicamus.
units.tr: 2. We judge this to be plainly necessary.

units.la: Confirmatio nostræ sententiæ.
units.tr: Confirmation of our view.

units.la: 1. Probationis loco, vel unicum 14.caput ad Corinthios esse potest, ubi Paulus eorum morem improbat, qui linguis peregrinis in Ecclesia loqui gaudebat. Et, cùm sermones, tùm preces peregrinis linguis, in publicis coetibus, peragetes, gravissimè reprehendit.
units.tr: 1. As proof, the 14th chapter of First Corinthians alone may suffice, where Paul disapproves of the custom of those who delighted in speaking in foreign tongues in the Church. Both sermons and prayers delivered in foreign tongues in public assemblies he rebukes most severely.

units.la: 2. Et sermones quod attinet, prophetiam, h.e. perspicuam & popularem interpretationem Scripturæ, multis modis, sermoni linguis peregrinis peracto, præstare, docet; quia prophetiâ populus ædificatur, linguis non item. Quod cùm proprio exemplo, tùm similî, à citharæ & tubæ incognito sono, illustrat v.1–32[?].
units.tr: 2. As for sermons, he teaches that prophecy, that is, clear and popular interpretation of Scripture, is in many ways better than a sermon delivered in a foreign tongue, because the people are edified by prophecy but not by tongues. He illustrates this both by his own example and by a similar one, from the sound of the lyre and the trumpet which is not understood, verses 1–32[?].

units.la: 3. Preces verò publicas, exotica linguâ peractas, eâdè ratione improbat, quia illis non intellectis nec ædificatur populus, nec Amen iisdem subjungêdo, adstipulari potest. v.13.14.15.16.
units.tr: 3. Public prayers offered in a strange language he disapproves on the same ground: since the people do not understand them, they are neither edified, nor can they join in by saying Amen to them. Verses 13, 14, 15, 16.

units.la: Assertio sententiæ nostræ contra Pon- tificiorum objectiones.
units.tr: Assertion of our view against the objections of the Papists.

units.la: Argumenta, seu [illegible, ~9 letters] potiùs, Papistarum, paucis quoque diluenda sunt.
units.tr: The arguments of the Papists, or rather their [illegible], must also be answered briefly.

units.la: 1. Verendum, ne rerum divinarum Majestas, linguâ vernaculâ apud plebem imminuatur.
units.tr: 1. It is to be feared that the majesty of divine things will be diminished if they are conducted in the vernacular before the common people.

units.la: R. Nulla est rationis hujus Consequentia; imò machinam hanc adversùs ipsos Verbi Dei hostes erigimus; certum quippe, majorem esse apud homines majestatem, verbi intellecti, quàm non intellecti. Sed & fallacia Accidentis subest; nec enim à lingua externa, sed à rerum præstantia & dignitate, majestas Verbi, dependet.
units.tr: Answer: This reasoning does not follow; indeed, we turn this very engine against the enemies of God's Word themselves. It is certain that the majesty of the Word is greater among men when it is understood than when it is not. But there is also a fallacy of accident here: the majesty of the Word depends not on an external language but on the excellence and dignity of the things themselves.

units.la: 2. Sacerdote sanctuarium ingrediente, populus Judaicus mansit foris. Ut igitur non opus erat, ut populus Sacerdotem precantem intelligeret; sic non necesse est, ut publicæ preces intelligantur.
units.tr: 2. When the priest entered the sanctuary, the Jewish people remained outside. Therefore, just as it was not necessary for the people to understand the priest praying, so it is not necessary that public prayers be understood.

units.la: R. Fallacia est falsorum parium: nec enim ab unico illo actu Sacerdotis, qui quotannis semel tantum, in typum ingressus Christi Domini in cœlum, ingressus est sanctuarium, consequentia valet, ad quotidianum Dei cultum, quem ipsi quoque V.T.Sacerdotes olim, lingua populo cognita, administrabant.
units.tr: Answer: This is a fallacy of false parallels. The inference does not hold from that single act of the priest, who entered the sanctuary only once a year, as a type of the entry of Christ the Lord into heaven, to the daily worship of God, which the Old Testament priests themselves once administered in a language known to the people.

units.la: 3. Populo non omnia communicanda, ne sanctum detur canibus. Matth.5.
units.tr: 3. Holy things should not be communicated to all the people, lest what is holy be given to dogs. Matt. 5.

units.la: R. Sic vero non satis est Pontificiis, populum Dei per contemtum, laicos appellare, nisi & canum numero illum accensent. Canum vero nomine Christus, nō coetus sacros, sed perversos sanctorum mysteriorum contemtores intelligit.
units.tr: Answer: It is not enough for the Papists to call the people of God laymen with contempt, unless they also count them among the dogs. By the name of dogs, however, Christ means not holy assemblies but perverse despisers of the holy mysteries.

units.la: 4. Facilius retinetur Ecclesiarum consensus, si unica aliqua communissima lingua, qualis est latina, sacra peragantur.
units.tr: 4. The agreement of the Churches is more easily kept if the sacred rites are performed in one common language, such as Latin.

units.la: R. Falsa est hæc assertio; nec enim linguarum, sed spiritus potius unitate, Ecclesiarum unio conservatur. Eph.4.1.2.
units.tr: Answer: This assertion is false. The unity of the Churches is preserved not by unity of language but rather by unity of the Spirit. Eph. 4.1, 2.

units.la: 5. Divinorum officiorum præcipuus finis, non est instructio populi, sed Dei cultus. Non igitur opus est, ut nota lingua peragantur.
units.tr: 5. The chief end of the divine offices is not the instruction of the people but the worship of God. There is therefore no need for them to be performed in a known language.

units.la: R. Plumbeus hic gladius est: quo tamen se ipsos feriunt hostes; fatentes, divina sua officia non ad instructionem facere: quòd si nihil faciunt ad instructionem, ergo nihil ad Dei quoque cultum: quî enim Deum colat populus, de eo nec institutus, nec ad cultum ejus instructus?
units.tr: Answer: This is a leaden sword, yet with it the enemies themselves strike themselves, for they confess that their divine offices do not serve for instruction. But if they do nothing for instruction, then they do nothing for the worship of God either: for how can the people worship God when they are neither taught about him nor trained for his worship?

units.la: 6. Sacerdos, tanquam caput, Ecclesiam suam repræsentat. Satis igitur est, si ipse sacra intelligat.
units.tr: 6. The priest, as the head, represents his Church. It is therefore enough that he himself understand the sacred rites.

units.la: R. Antecedens vanam Sacrificulorum sapit jactantiam; nec enim, proprie loquendo, aliud Ecclesiæ caput est, quàm Christus. Falsa quinetiam est Consequentia; cùm enim Sacerdotis, quem Ministrum Christi appellare malumus, officium sit populo præire, omninò à populo intelligi debet.
units.tr: Answer: The antecedent savours of the vain boasting of the sacrificers; for, properly speaking, the head of the Church is none other than Christ. The inference is moreover false: since the office of the priest, whom we prefer to call the minister of Christ, is to go before the people, it must surely be understood by the people.

units.la: 7. Satis est, si, quæ peragantur, Deus intelligat: satis quinetiam, si populus sacra ad Dei laudem fieri, sciat.
units.tr: 7. It is enough if God understands what is performed; indeed it is enough if the people know that the sacred rites are performed to the praise of God.

units.la: R. Utrumque falsum est: non satis est Deum sacra publica intelligere; quia populus ædificandus est, & sic orandum, ut populus Amen possit subjungere. 1.Cor.14. Nec sufficit, si populus sciat, ad Dei laudem fieri, quæ fiunt, sed necesse est, ipse quoque Deum celebret. Adhæc, quomodo Deum vel laudari, vel blasphemari sciet, si nihil eorum, quæ fiunt, intelligit?
units.tr: Answer: Both are false. It is not enough that God understands the public sacred rites, because the people must be edified, and so must pray in such a way that the people can say Amen. 1 Cor. 14. Nor is it sufficient if the people know that what is done is done to God's praise; rather it is necessary that they themselves also praise God. Moreover, how will they know whether God is praised or blasphemed if they understand none of what is done?

units.la: DISPUTATIO QUINTA. In qua DE S. SCRIPTURÆ INTERPRETATIONE.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO QUINTA. In which concerning the interpretation of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Status Controversiæ.
units.tr: The State of the Controversy.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Hoc unicè agunt Pontificii, ut ovibus Christi, vitæ pabulum subducant, ἀτροφίαν, extremamque tabem accersant. Quòd si igitur, Sacra Biblia nobis è manibus eripi non posse, animadvertunt, omnes tamen nervos eò intendunt, ut jus interpretandi Scripturam, soli Ecclesiæ Romanæ, imò soli Pontifici, vendicent.
units.tr: The Papists work single-mindedly at this: they cut off the food of life from Christ's sheep, and bring on wasting and final decay. And so, since they notice that the Holy Bible cannot be snatched from our hands, they nevertheless bend all their sinews toward claiming for the Roman Church alone, indeed for the Pope alone, the right to interpret Scripture.

units.la: 2. Hinc eò impudentiæ deveniunt, ut nec privatis fidelibus, nec Principibus & Regibus, jus inquirendi, in fidei dogmata, aut de illis ex Scriptura judicandi, concedant.
units.tr: 2. From this they proceed to such shamelessness that they grant neither to private believers nor to princes and kings the right to inquire into the doctrines of faith, or to judge about them from Scripture.

units.la: 3. Nec verò sine specioso prætextu hoc faciunt, Scripturam variis sensibus obnoxiam, ideoque obscuram, & vix etiam doctissimis explicabilem esse, fingunt & contendunt.
units.tr: 3. Nor do they do this without a specious pretext: they invent and contend that Scripture is open to various senses, and therefore obscure, and hardly explicable even by the most learned.

units.la: 4. Tres igitur, hac Disputatione, Quæstiones ordine pertractandæ.
units.tr: 4. Therefore three questions are to be treated in order in this Disputation:

units.la: I. Sit ne unus an plures S. Scripturæ sensus?
units.tr: I. Is there one sense of Holy Scripture, or several?

units.la: II. Liceat ne laicis quoque in dogmata Religionis inquirere, eaq; ex Dei verbo judicare?
units.tr: II. May laymen also inquire into the doctrines of religion, and judge them by the Word of God?

units.la: III. Quis supremus Scripturæ interpretandæ, controversiarum &[?] dijudicandarum sit Judex?
units.tr: III. Who is the supreme judge of Scripture's interpretation and of the deciding of controversies?

units.la: DE PRIMA QUÆSTIONE.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE FIRST QUESTION.

units.la: Sententia Papistarum.
units.tr: The Opinion of the Papists.

units.la: 1. Pontificii varios Scripturæ sensus affingunt.
units.tr: 1. The Papists attribute to Scripture various senses.

units.la: 2. Bellarminus l.de Verbo Dei 3.cap.3. duplicem sæpenumero, loci cujuspiam sensum esse, docet, Literalem & Spiritualem.
units.tr: 2. Bellarmine, in his book on the Word of God, book 3, chapter 3, teaches that very often there is a twofold sense of any passage, the literal and the spiritual.

units.la: 3. Literalem vocat, quem verba immediatè præ se ferunt, eumque pro verborum proprietate aut translatione, simplicem aut figuratum nominat, statuitque, in una eademque sententia sæpe plures literales sensus reperiri.
units.tr: 3. He calls the literal the sense which the words immediately present, and he names it simple or figurative according as the words are used in their proper or a transferred meaning; and he holds that in one and the same statement several literal senses are often found.

units.la: 4. Spiritualem verò nominat, qui aliò referitur, quàm ad id, quod verba immediatè significant. Quem Patres quidem communiter allegoricum dixerint, recentiores verò Theologi distinguunt, in Allegoricum, quo verba præter literalem sensum, significent aliquid in Novo Test. de Christo aut Ecclesia: in Tropologicum, quo verba aut facta ad mores referantur: in Anagogicum denique, quo verba aut facta referantur ad significandam vitam æternam. Atque hunc sensum, non in omnibus Scripturæ sententiis reperiri testatur Bellarm. capite suprà dicto.
units.tr: 4. The spiritual sense, however, he names the sense that refers to something other than what the words immediately signify. The Fathers commonly called this the allegorical, but more recent theologians distinguish it into the allegorical, by which the words, beyond the literal sense, signify something about Christ or the Church in the New Testament; the tropological, by which words or deeds are referred to morals; and finally the anagogical, by which words or deeds are referred to signifying eternal life. Bellarmine, in the chapter cited above, testifies that this sense is not found in all statements of Scripture.

units.la: 5. Addit idem Bell. His ita constitutis, convenit inter nos & adversarios, ex solo literali sensu peti debere argumenta; nam eum solum Spiritus S. sensum esse, qui ex verbis immediatè colligitur.
units.tr: 5. The same Bellarmine adds: With these things thus established, it is agreed between us and our opponents that arguments must be drawn from the literal sense alone; for that alone is the sense of the Holy Spirit which is gathered immediately from the words.

units.la: Nostra sententia.
units.tr: Our Opinion.

units.la: 1. Nos postremum illud Bellarmini effatum, ambabus ulnis, amplectimur, nempe argumenta ex solo literali sensu petenda; eum nimirum Spiritus S. sensum esse, qui ex verbis immediatè colligitur; agnoscimus quippe & nos, Theologiam symbolicam, non esse argumentativam.
units.tr: 1. We embrace with both arms that last saying of Bellarmine, namely that arguments are to be drawn from the literal sense alone; that is, that sense alone is the sense of the Holy Spirit which is gathered immediately from the words. For we too acknowledge that symbolic theology is not argumentative.

units.la: 2. Hinc ita argumentamur: Is tantùm cujusque loci sensus est, qui Spiritus S. sensus est, & ex quo argumenta petenda. Atqui solus literalis talis est. Ergo solus cujusq; loci sensus est. Minor est Bellarmini: Major indubiæ veritatis est; ut enim Scriptura vox Spiritus sancti est, ita sensus ejus is tantùm est, qui Spiritus sancti proprius est.
units.tr: 2. Hence we argue thus: That alone is the sense of each passage which is the sense of the Holy Spirit, and from which arguments are to be drawn. But only the literal sense is such. Therefore only the literal is the sense of each passage. The minor premise is Bellarmine's; the major is of undoubted truth. For just as the words of Scripture are the voice of the Holy Spirit, so its sense is only that which belongs properly to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 3. Quòd si literalis tantùm sensus Spiritus sancti proprius est, solus igitur divinus est, solus pro vero ac genuino habendus.
units.tr: 3. But if only the literal sense belongs properly to the Holy Spirit, then it alone is divine, and alone is to be held as true and genuine.

units.la: 4. Literalem autem sensum nos eum esse dicimus, quem verba contextus, seu propria illa, seu figurata fuerint, immediatè indigitant.
units.tr: 4. We say, moreover, that the literal sense is that which the words of the context immediately point to, whether they are used properly or figuratively.

units.la: 5. Sensus hic, in unaquaque sententia unicus est; nec enim obstat, quòd verba textus propria sint aut figurata; unitas enim sensus non tam ex nudis verbis, quàm ex unitate scopi & re significata pendet. Unde in parabolarum quoque explicatione, non tam ad singula verba & minimos quosque apices, quàm ad scopum & materiam subjectam respiciendum.
units.tr: 5. This sense is single in every statement; for it is no objection that the words of the text are proper or figurative. For the unity of sense depends not so much on bare words as on the unity of the aim and of the thing signified. Hence also in the explanation of parables we must look not so much to the individual words and the smallest points, as to the aim and the subject matter.

units.la: 6. Neque unitati sensus officit, quòd in Veteri Testamento, plurimæ sententiæ, ex historiâ & typo, seu mysterio Christum concernente, compositæ leguntur, unde vulgò sensus simplex aut compositus dicitur; nec enim sensus compositus, alius est quàm literalis, siquidem verba immediatè & historiam & typum indigitant.
units.tr: 6. Nor does the unity of sense stand in the way of the fact that in the Old Testament many statements are read that are composed of history and type, or mystery concerning Christ; whence it is commonly called a simple or composite sense. For a composite sense is no different from the literal, since the words immediately point to both the history and the type.

units.la: 7. Ut verò non in quavis sententia, typus fingendus est: ita, ubi præter historiam, typum quoque esse, vel ex ipsis verbis contextus, (ut in promissione Salomonis & Christi, 2.Sam.7.) vel ex loci in N.Testamento interpretatione (ut in dicto Oseæ 11.1.Matth.2.citato) necessariò cócluditur, non minùs ex typo, quàm ex historia in rebus fidei argumentari licet.
units.tr: 7. But just as a type is not to be invented in every statement, so where, besides the history, a type is also necessarily concluded either from the words of the context itself (as in the promise of Solomon and Christ, 2 Sam. 7) or from the interpretation of a passage in the New Testament (as in the cited saying of Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2), it is lawful to argue in matters of faith no less from the type than from the history.

units.la: Assertio nostræ sententiæ.
units.tr: Confirmation of Our Opinion.

units.la: 1. Veritas sententiæ nostræ, ex præcedentibus, satis est manifesta. Papistarum argumenta paucis quoque refutanda sunt.
units.tr: 1. The truth of our opinion is sufficiently clear from what has gone before. The Papists' arguments must also be refuted briefly.

units.la: 2. Pugnant autem pro sensu spirituali, exemplis.
units.tr: 2. They fight for a spiritual sense by examples.

units.la: Allegorici sensus exemplum esse dicunt, in historia Abrahami, Saræ & Agar, Isaaci & Ismaëlis. Gal.4.
units.tr: They say that an example of the allegorical sense is in the history of Abraham, Sarah and Hagar, Isaac and Ishmael. Gal. 4.

units.la: Tropologici exemplum esse statuunt, illud Deut.25. Non obligabis os bovi triturânti, quod ad literam de bobus, spiritualiter de Ministris intelligendum. 1.Cor.9.
units.tr: They hold that an example of the tropological sense is that in Deut. 25: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, which, according to the letter, is to be understood of oxen, but spiritually of ministers. 1 Cor. 9.

units.la: Anagogici verò sensus exemplum faciunt, illud Psal.94. Quibus juravi in ira mea, si introibunt in requiem meam, quod ad literam de terra promissionis intellectum, spiritualiter ad vitam æternam accommodat Apostolus Heb.4.
units.tr: And they make an example of the anagogical sense of that in Psalm 94: To whom I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest, which, understood according to the letter of the land of promise, the Apostle applies spiritually to eternal life. Heb. 4.

units.la: [?]R. Nequaquam hinc cõficitur, cujus quam loci alium quàm literalem sensum esse. Allegoricum enim sensum quod attinet, non alius is est, quàm literalis compositus, cujus exemplum est Gal.4. Unde falsa est divisio sensus, in literalem & spiritualem, quia spiritualis nihil, quàm sensus literalis compositi pars est. In cæteris mirè confundunt sensum Scripturæ, cum varia ejus interpretatione, usu, & accommodatione. Quid? non ne Scriptura utilis est, πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, πρὸς ἐλεγχον, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, πρὸς παιδείαν, &, ut ex Rom.15. liquet, πρὸς παράκλησιν? sed num ideò tot sensus erunt, quot accómodationes ad usum? Ec quis verò non manifestè videat, tropologicum & anagogicum usum potiùs, quàm sensum, sub enumeratis Scripturæ utilitatibus contineri? Legem divinam, Bovem triturantem non capistrabis, in literali & nativo sensu citat & Ministris accommodat Apostolus. Sensus autem ille figuratis quidem verbis expressus, nullus alius est, quàm operarium mercede non fraudandum. Nec Heb.4. juramento divino, Si ingressi fuerint in requiem meam, alium sensum tribuit, sed comparatione Christianorum, cum Israëlitis facta, monet, ne nos æternâ requie privemus, sicut illi se ipsos terrâ promissâ. Quòd si maximè compositum sensum esse dicamus, non tamen sequetur, illum literalem non esse.
units.tr: [?]Answer. It by no means follows from this that there is any sense of any passage other than the literal. For as far as the allegorical sense is concerned, it is not other than the literal composite sense, of which Gal. 4 is an example. Hence the division of sense into literal and spiritual is false, because the spiritual is nothing but a part of the composite literal sense. In the rest they wonderfully confuse the sense of Scripture with its various interpretation, use, and application. What? Is not Scripture useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, for instruction, and, as is clear from Rom. 15, for comfort? But will there therefore be as many senses as there are applications to use? And who does not clearly see that the tropological and anagogical are rather uses than senses, contained under the enumerated uses of Scripture? The Apostle cites the divine law, You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, in its literal and native sense, and applies it to ministers. But that sense, expressed in figurative words, is none other than that a workman is not to be defrauded of his wages. Nor does Heb. 4 assign another sense to the divine oath, If they shall enter into my rest, but by comparing Christians with the Israelites warns that we should not deprive ourselves of eternal rest, as they deprived themselves of the promised land. But even if we should say that the sense is most of all composite, it does not follow that it is not literal.

units.la: De Secunda Quæstione. Status Controversiæ.
units.tr: On the Second Question. The State of the Controversy.

units.la: 1. Quæstio hæc, cum superiori, An Scriptura in linguâ vernaculâ, à quibusvis Christianis legenda sit? maximam partem coincidit. Brevius itaque hîc agendum.
units.tr: 1. This question largely coincides with the previous one, namely, whether Scripture ought to be read in the vernacular by any Christians whatsoever. I shall therefore treat it more briefly here.

units.la: 2. Papani hanc libertatem, inquirendi in doctrinam & de illa ex Scripturis judicandi, laicis denegant.
units.tr: 2. The Papists deny laypeople this liberty: the liberty to inquire into doctrine and to judge it from the Scriptures.

units.la: 3. Nos verò eam illis tribuimus & asserimus.
units.tr: 3. We, however, grant and assert this liberty to them.

units.la: Sententiæ nostræ confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation of our view.

units.la: Duo cumprimis argumenta proferimus.
units.tr: We bring forward two arguments above all.

units.la: 1. Necessitatem: quòd laicos quoque de doctrina judicare oporteat. ut testantur loca, quibus omnes fideles jubentur, sibi à seductoribus cavere, spiritus discernere, omniaque probare. Matth.7.15. 1.Thess.5.17.& 1.Joh.4.1.
units.tr: 1. The necessity: that laypeople too ought to judge doctrine, as the passages testify, in which all the faithful are commanded to beware of seducers, to test the spirits, and to prove all things. Matt. 7:15; 1 Thess. 5:17 (sic, 5:21); and 1 John 4:1.

units.la: 2. Facultatem: quòd Laici Dei gratiâ hoc quoque possint. Quò faciunt loca Scripturæ, quibus Spiritus sanctus, non certo hominum ordini, sed quibusvis, juxta certam mensuram promittitur. Efaiæ 54.11. Jer.31.33. Joh.6.45. & 10.27. Eph.4.7. Tit.3.6.
units.tr: 2. The ability: that laypeople, by the grace of God, are able to do this too. To this purpose the passages of Scripture point, in which the Holy Spirit is promised not to a fixed order of men, but to whomever, according to a certain measure. Isa. 54:11; Jer. 31:33; John 6:45 and 10:27; Eph. 4:7; Titus 3:6.

units.la: Argumenta Pontificiorum, subsequenti Quæstione discutientur: pergendum itaque.
units.tr: The arguments of the Papists will be examined in the following question; let us therefore proceed.

units.la: De Tertia Quæstione. Pontificiorum sententia.
units.tr: On the Third Question. The opinion of the Papists.

units.la: 1. Tertia, eaque præcipua, Quæstio est de summo Scripturæ interpretandæ Judice.
units.tr: 1. The third question, and the chief one, is concerning the supreme judge of the interpretation of Scripture.

units.la: 2. Convenit, inquit Bellarminus, l.3.de Verbo Dei,c.3. inter nos & adversarios, Scripturas intelligi debere eo Spiritu, quo facta sunt, i.e.Spiritu sancto. Quod Apostolus Petrus epist.2.c.1.docet, cum ait: Hoc primùm intelligentes, quòd omnis prophetia Scripturæ propriâ interpretatione non fit: Nō enim humanâ voluntate allata est aliquando prophetia, sed Spiritu S. inspirati, loquuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Ubi B.Petrus probat, non debere exponi Scripturas ex proprio ingenio, sed secundùm dictamen Spiritus sancti, quia non sint scripta humano ingenio, sed ex inspiratione Spiritus sancti. Hactenus Bell. Utinam verò ita syncerè sentiret: sed audi, quibus jam strophis utatur Jesuita.
units.tr: 2. "We agree," says Bellarmine, book 3 On the Word of God, chapter 3, "between us and our opponents, that the Scriptures ought to be understood by the same Spirit by which they were made, that is, by the Holy Spirit. This the Apostle Peter teaches in 2 Peter 1, when he says: 'Knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation. For prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.' Here St. Peter proves that Scriptures ought not to be expounded according to one's own wit, but according to the dictate of the Holy Spirit, because they were not written by human wit, but by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit." Thus far Bellarmine. Would that he meant this so sincerely! But listen to the verses the Jesuit now employs.

units.la: 3. Tota igitur, inquit, quæstio est, ubi sit ille Spiritus? Nos enim existimamus hunc Spiritum, etsi multis privatis hominibus conceditur, tamen certò inveniri in Ecclesia. In qua verò Ecclesia? subdit, Id est, in Concilio Episcoporum, confirmato à summo Pastore, sive in summo Pastore, cum Concilio aliorum Pastorum.
units.tr: 3. "The whole question, then," he says, "is where that Spirit is? For we hold that this Spirit, although it is granted to many private men, is nevertheless certainly found in the Church." In which Church? He adds: "That is, in the council of bishops, confirmed by the supreme Pastor, or in the supreme Pastor together with the council of the other pastors."

units.la: 4. Quæ omnia si probè excusserimus, judicandi potestas erit penes Ecclesiam. Ecclesiæ nomine intelligetur Concilium Episcoporum. Concilium nullum aliud, nisi quod à Papa confirmatum. Et consequenter sub Ecclesiæ & Conciliorum titulo, Papa, cujus judicium, de Religione, si Bellarmino, l.3.de Pontif.Rom.c.2. creditur, prorsus est infallibile.
units.tr: 4. If we examine all this carefully, the power of judging will rest with the Church. By the name of the Church will be understood the council of bishops; and no council other than one confirmed by the Pope. And consequently, under the title of the Church and of the councils, the Pope is meant, whose judgment on religion, if we believe Bellarmine, book 3 On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 2, is altogether infallible.

units.la: Nostra sententia.
units.tr: Our opinion.

units.la: 1. Nos verò istam Papistarum sententiam, tanquam impiam & periculosam, damnamus : nec alium Scripturae interpretandae Judicem quàm Scripturam & Spiritum S. h.e.Spiritum S. foris in Scripturis loquentem & suadentem, intus vero in corde operantem & persuadentem, agnoscimus.
units.tr: 1. We, however, condemn this opinion of the Papists as impious and dangerous, and we acknowledge no other judge of the interpretation of Scripture than Scripture itself and the Holy Spirit: that is, the Holy Spirit speaking and urging outwardly in the Scriptures, and inwardly working in the heart and persuading.

units.la: 2. Similiter in dijudicandis controversiis sola Scriptura sacra, regula est, quâ rectum ab incurvo discernitur : libella & norma, quâ Spiritualis aedificii rectitudo examinatur: pixidula nautica, quâ Christi navicula dirigitur : lydius denique lapis, quo aenea ab aureis & falsa à veris dignoscuntur.
units.tr: 2. Likewise, in deciding controversies, Holy Scripture alone is the rule by which the straight is distinguished from the crooked; the level and the square by which the rectitude of the spiritual building is tested; the mariner's compass by which Christ's little ship is steered; and finally the touchstone by which bronze is distinguished from gold and the false from the true.

units.la: 3. Interea neque Ecclesiae judicium, neque Conciliorum placita improbamus, sed tanquam media interpretationis acceptamus, dummodo non Ecclesiae vox ad Romanam adstringatur, sicque scortum pro virgine, malignantium conciliabula pro legitimis Conciliis obtrudantur, summumque interpretandi jus non Ecclesiae, sed Spiritui S. reservetur.
units.tr: 3. Meanwhile we do not reject the judgment of the Church or the decisions of councils, but accept them as means of interpretation, provided that the voice of the Church is not confined to the Roman one, and thus a harlot is not foisted upon us for a virgin, and the conventicles of evil men for lawful councils, and the supreme right of interpreting is reserved not to the Church but to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 4. Meminisse autem debemus, nos nec Scripturam sine Spiritu, nec Spiritum sine Scriptura Judicem dicere. Illud enim impium foret & contrarium divinae promissioni Ef.59.21. ubi Verbum Dei & Spiritus, indivulso nexu, junguntur. Hoc vero Enthusiastarum errorem saperet.
units.tr: 4. We must remember, however, that we call neither Scripture without the Spirit nor the Spirit without Scripture the judge. For the former would be impious and contrary to the divine promise, Isa. 59:21, where the Word of God and the Spirit are joined in an unbroken bond. The latter would smack of the error of the Enthusiasts.

units.la: 5. Quin imò, quia Spiritus, in Scriptura loquens, audiendus est: media interpretationis legitima sunt: Invocatio Spiritus S. frequens: assidua lectio: linguarum cognitio & fontium inspectio: verborum propriorum & figuratorum distinctio: argumenti, scopi, circumstantiarum, antecedentium & consequentium, observatio: obscurorum cum clarioribus, similium cum similibus, dissimilium cum dissimilibus collatio, & denique fidei analogia.
units.tr: 5. Indeed, because the Spirit, speaking in Scripture, must be heard, the means of interpretation are lawful: frequent invocation of the Holy Spirit; constant reading; knowledge of languages and inspection of the sources; the distinction of proper and figurative words; observation of the subject matter, the aim, the circumstances, and what precedes and follows; the comparison of obscure passages with clearer ones, of similar with similar, and of dissimilar with dissimilar; and finally the analogy of faith.

units.la: Nostrae sententiae confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation of our view.

units.la: Rationes pro nostra & contra Papistarum sententiam sunt evidentissimae.
units.tr: The reasons for our view and against the opinion of the Papists are most evident.

units.la: 1. Quia in omni controversia Religionis, non solùm privati, sed Sacerdotes ac Pastores, sicut & Reges & Principes, ad Scripturam, tanquam normam, remittuntur. Deut.4.2. & 12.32. & 17.10. Josuae 1.8. Esaiae 8.20. Malachiae 2.7. & 4.4. Joh.5.39. 1.Tim.4.13.
units.tr: 1. Because in every controversy of religion, not only private persons but also priests and pastors, as well as kings and princes, are referred to Scripture as the rule. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; 17:10; Josh. 1:8; Isa. 8:20; Mal. 2:7; 4:4; John 5:39; 1 Tim. 4:13.

units.la: 2. Quia testantur id ipsum Exempla, Davidis, Salomonis, Ezechiae, Josiae, &c. In N.T. Beroënsium, Act.17. Fidelium, de quibus 2.Pet.1.19. Inprimis autem Christi, qui Pharisaeos ex Scripturis refutavit, & ad Scripturam Vet.Test. provocavit. Joh.5.17.
units.tr: 2. Because the examples bear witness to this very thing: those of David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Josiah, and so on. In the New Testament, the Bereans of Acts 17, the faithful of whom 2 Peter 1:19 speaks, and above all Christ himself, who refuted the Pharisees from the Scriptures and appealed to the Old Testament Scripture. John 5:17 (sic, 5:39).

units.la: 3. Supremi Judicis est, nunquam errare, & infallibiliter verum dicere: nullo partium studio duci, veritatemque cordibus hominum sic ingenerare, ut in ejus sententia tutò conquiescere posint [?]. At nulla Ecclesia visibilis, nullum Concilium aut Episcopus dari potest, in quem haec competant. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 3. It belongs to the supreme Judge never to err and to speak what is true infallibly, to be led by no partisan zeal, and so to engender the truth in the hearts of men that they may safely rest in his sentence. But no visible Church, no council, or bishop can be given in whom these qualities belong. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 4. Si Scriptura est vox Spiritus S., nusquam tutius, quàm in Scripturis, inquiritur, nusquam certius invenitur. Prius est, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: 4. If Scripture is the voice of the Holy Spirit, nowhere is it more safely sought than in the Scriptures, and nowhere is it more certainly found. The antecedent is true, therefore also the consequent.

units.la: 5. Unicus noster Magister & Doctor Christus in Scripturis dicitur, Matth.17.5.& 23.8.10. Joh.10.2. E. Nemo hominum pro supremo Scripturae Judice agnoscendus est.
units.tr: 5. Our only Master and Teacher, Christ, is named in the Scriptures, Matt. 17:5; 23:8, 10; John 10:2. Therefore no human being is to be acknowledged as the supreme judge of Scripture.

units.la: 6. Si Romana Ecclesia, Concilium aut Pontifex, pro supremo Judice haberi debet: tum fides nostra in hominem terminabitur & ultimò resolvetur, sicque fides tantùm humano nitetur arbitrio. Posterius absurdum est; sic enim Religio everteretur, & Atheismo fenestra aperiretur. Ergo absurdum quoque est prius.
units.tr: 6. If the Roman Church, a council, or the Pope must be held as the supreme judge, then our faith would terminate in a man and finally rest upon him, and thus faith would lean only upon human judgment. The latter is absurd; for in this way religion would be overthrown, and a window opened to atheism. Therefore the former is absurd too.

units.la: 7. Subscribunt Patres quoque. August.de nuptiis, lib.2.33. adversus Pelagianos: Controversia Judicem requirit, judicet igitur Christus, & cui rei mors ejus profuerit, ipse dicat. Hic est, inquit, sanguis meus, qui pro multis effundetur, in remissionem peccatorum. Judicet cum illo Apostolus, quia & in Apostolo loquitur Christus, &c. Et adversus Donatistas passim, inquit: Non audiamus haec dicit, haec dico, sed audiamus haec dicit Dominus. Item libro de Past. Ibi (nempe in Scripturis) pascite, quicquid inde audiveritis, hoc bene vobis sapiat, quicquid extra est, respuite, colligite vos ad montes Scripturae sanctae. lib.2.de Lib.Arb.& Gratia,32.cap. Literas Cypriani non ut canonicas habeo, sed ex canonicis considero, & quod in eis divinarum Scripturarum autoritati convenit, cum laude ejus accipio, quod non convenit, cum pace ejus respuo. Chrysost.2.Cor.hom.13. Habemus exactissimam trutinam, gnomonem & regulam, divinarum legum observationem. Ideo obsecro vos, omittatis, quod huic aut illi videatur: verum a Scripturis omnia haec inquirite.
units.tr: The Fathers also subscribe. Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, chapter 33, against the Pelagians: "Controversy requires a judge. Let Christ therefore judge, and let him himself say what his death has profited. 'This is my blood,' he says, 'which shall be shed for many, for the remission of sins.' Let the Apostle judge with him, because Christ speaks also in the Apostle, etc." And against the Donatists he says everywhere: "Let us not listen to 'this one says,' 'I say this,' but let us listen to 'thus says the Lord.'" Likewise in his book On Pastors: "There feed (namely in the Scriptures); whatever you hear from there, let it taste well to you; whatever is outside it, reject; gather yourselves to the mountains of holy Scripture." Book 2 On Free Will and Grace, chapter 32: "I do not hold the letters of Cyprian as canonical, but I consider them by the canonical ones, and what in them agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures I accept with praise of it; what does not agree I reject with his peace." Chrysostom, homily 13 on 2 Corinthians: "We have a most exact balance, a gnomon and a rule, the observance of the divine laws. Therefore I beg you, set aside what seems so to this one or that one; rather, inquire into all these things from the Scriptures."

units.la: Assertio nostræ sententiæ contra ob- jectiones Pontificiorum.
units.tr: Assertion of our position against the objections of the Papists.

units.la: 1. Abutuntur testimoniis Veteris Testamenti,quibus Pontifices spiritualium controversiarum judices constituuntur. Sic enim Exod.18.23. Moses de omnibus controversiis respondisse dicitur. Deut.17.10. Facies quod Sacerdos dixerit. Sic Eccl.12.11. Hag.2.12. Malach.2.7.
units.tr: 1. They misuse the testimonies of the Old Testament by which the Pontiffs are appointed judges of spiritual controversies. For Exodus 18:23 says: Moses is said to have answered concerning all controversies. Deuteronomy 17:10: You shall do what the priest has said. So also Ecclesiastes 12:11; Haggai 2:12; Malachi 2:7.

units.la: R. I. His testimoniis non probatur, Pontificibus supremum judicium, in omnibus controversiis, commissum fuisse; audiendi quidem erant, sed non nisi secundùm legem judicantes, cujus custodes erant, Malach.2.6.7. II. Confunduntur personæ, quarum non est eadem ratio: Moses non Sacerdos, sed Judex, populi Dei, fuit. Nec tam de Religionis controversiis, quàm de forensibus litibus sonat illud Exod.18.23.
units.tr: Answer. I. These testimonies do not prove that the supreme judgment in all controversies was committed to the Pontiffs. They were indeed to be heard, but they were to judge only according to the law, whose guardians they were (Malachi 2:6-7). II. Different persons are confused, who do not have the same standing: Moses was not a priest but a judge of the people of God. Nor does that passage of Exodus 18:23 refer so much to controversies of religion as to ordinary lawsuits.

units.la: 2. Petro & successoribus ejus commissum est judicium de controversiis fidei. Ergo & Ecclesiæ Romanæ ejusque capiti. Antecedens probant ex variis prærogativis Petro concessis. Matth.16.v.19. Tibi dabo claves, &c. & Matth.18.17. Dic Ecclesiæ. Joh.21.16. Pasce oves meas, &c.
units.tr: 2. The judgment concerning controversies of faith was committed to Peter and his successors. Therefore also to the Church of Rome and its head. They prove the antecedent from various prerogatives granted to Peter: Matthew 16:19, I will give you the keys, etc.; Matthew 18:17, Tell it to the Church; John 21:16, Feed my sheep, etc.

units.la: R. I. Falsum est Antecedens; nihil enim hujusmodi ex dictis locis conficitur. II. Falsa est Consequentia, à Petro ad Romanum Pontificem; Non hæreditatem Petri habet, qui ejus fidem non habet, præclarè inquit Ambrosius.
units.tr: Answer. I. The antecedent is false; for nothing of this kind follows from the said passages. II. The consequence from Peter to the Roman Pontiff is false: He does not have the inheritance of Peter who does not have his faith, as Ambrose rightly says.

units.la: 3. Controversia de circumcisione in Concilio Hierof.decisa est, Act.15. & in Ecclesiastica historia multa talia leguntur. Ergo hodieque hic modus tenendus.
units.tr: 3. The controversy about circumcision was decided in the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), and many such things are read in ecclesiastical history. Therefore this method must be kept today as well.

units.la: R. Negatur, controversias à Conciliis tanquam summo Judice decisas esse; quod enim ad Concilium Hierof.,contrarium plane testatur Lucas v.15. Huic ait consonant verba Prophetarum. & v.28. Visum est Spiritui S. & nobis.
units.tr: Answer. It is denied that controversies were decided by councils as the supreme judge; for Luke clearly testifies to the contrary concerning the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15:15, To this the words of the Prophets agree, and 15:28, It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.

units.la: 4. Privatus spiritus non est audiendus.1.Joh.4.v.1. Ergo potiùs audiendus summus Ecclesiæ Pontifex.
units.tr: 4. A private spirit is not to be heard (1 John 4:1). Therefore the supreme Pontiff of the Church is rather to be heard.

units.la: R. I. Pro summo Ecclesiæ Pontifice nemo, nisi Christus, agnoscendus est. II. Antecedens calumniousum est; nec enim privatum cujusque spiritum, sed Spiritum in Scripturis loquentem, Judicem dicimus.
units.tr: Answer. I. No one, except Christ, is to be acknowledged as the supreme Pontiff of the Church. II. The antecedent is calumnious; for we do not call judge the private spirit of each person, but the Spirit speaking in the Scriptures.

units.la: 5. Judex externus & visibilis esse debet, qui ab omnibus conspiciatur & audiatur, & praeterea autoritatem coactivam habeat. At talis non est Scriptura. Ergo.
units.tr: 5. The external and visible judge must be one who is seen and heard by all, and moreover has a coercive authority. But Scripture is not such. Therefore.

units.la: R. In Majore cavenda est confusio Judicis spiritualis, cum humano & corporali: normalis cum personali. Minor vero falsa est, simpliciter accepta. Nam Spiritus S. in Scriptura lectâ & audita, ab omnibus auditur, & autoritatem habet coactivam, non tyrannicam, sed efficacem, ad instituendum pios & convincendum impios.
units.tr: Answer. In the major premise, the confusion of a spiritual judge with a human and bodily one must be guarded against, and of a normal judge with a personal one. The minor premise, taken simply, is false. For the Holy Spirit, in Scripture read and heard, is heard by all, and has a coercive authority, not tyrannical but effective, for instructing the godly and convicting the ungodly.

units.la: 6. Scriptura est ipsa litis materia. Ergo non potest esse Judex. Ratio ; quia nemo simul Reus & Judex, aut sui ipsius Judex est.
units.tr: 6. Scripture is itself the matter of the dispute. Therefore it cannot be the judge. The reason: no one is at once defendant and judge, or judge of himself.

units.la: R. Falsum est Antecedens; nō enim Scriptura ipsa, sed variae Scripturae interpretationes & controversiae, litis sunt materia. Sed & Consequentia laborat; etsi enim in judiciis humanis, nemo de se ipso testari aut judicare queat, alia tamen est ratio Judicis divini, qui cum mentiri nequeat, testis est omni exceptione major.
units.tr: Answer. The antecedent is false; for it is not Scripture itself, but the various interpretations and controversies about Scripture, that are the matter of the dispute. The consequence also fails; for although in human judgments no one can bear witness or judge concerning himself, the case of the divine Judge is otherwise, who, since he cannot lie, is a witness greater than any objection.
